5S of Housekeeping 5S is a workplace organization / housekeeping method that uses five Japanese words, all starting with the letter S: seiri, seiton, seiso, seiketsu, shitsuke . It was developed in Japan as part of the Toyota Production System (anglicized as Lean ) and is usually the first lean method organizations implement. The goal: "a place for everything and everything in its place." 5S reduces waste and optimizes productivity by maintaining an orderly workplace and using visual cues (signs, labels, floor markings, color codes) for more consistent operational results. The 5S methodology (Nikita Klyuchko / Respublika Narodnaya, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA) The 5S "onion" diagram (Rafabitu, Wikimedia Commons, public domain) The Five S's Japanese English What it means Seiri Sort Separate needed from unneeded items (tools, parts, materials, paperwork) and discard the unneeded Seiton Set in Order Neatly arrange what is left — a place for everything and everything in its place Seiso Shine Clean the workplace and equipment thoroughly Seiketsu Standardize Standardize the way the first three S's are done so cleanliness is maintained Shitsuke Sustain Discipline — keep following the first four S's without being told 1. Seiri (Sort) Sorting through all items in a work area and removing everything not needed for current operations. Make work easier by eliminating obstacles. Best-known tool: red tagging — a red tag is placed on every item that isn't needed (or isn't in the right location/quantity) so it can be evaluated and removed. Remove items that are broken, unusable, or only occasionally used. 2. Seiton (Set in Order) Put all necessary items in the optimal place for fulfilling their function — organize for efficient use. Arrange tools/parts so they can be easily picked for use; put frequently used items near the operator. Prevents loss and wasted time searching; makes it easy to spot missing or misplaced items. Uses labels, shadow boards, floor marking, and color coding so items are easy to find AND easy to return. Principle: "Can See, Can Take Out, Can Return." 3. Seiso (Shine) Clean the workplace completely — sweep, dust, polish. Use cleaning as inspection: while cleaning, you spot problems, leaks, and equipment deterioration early. Identify and eliminate the sources of dirt and grime (remove the need to clean). Divide areas into cleaning zones and assign ownership/responsibilities. 4. Seiketsu (Standardize) Standardize the processes by which Seiri, Seiton, and Seiso are done every day to keep the workplace in perfect condition. Tools: job cycle charts, visual cues (signs, placards, scoreboards), scheduled "five-minute" 5S periods, checklists, and 5S audit sheets. Assign 5S job responsibilities and integrate them into regular work duties. 5. Shitsuke (Sustain) Form the habit of always following the first four S's without being told — discipline. The hardest S: human nature resists change and drifts back to "the old way." Sustained through regular training, routine 5S audits, management setting the example, and making 5S part of daily routine (a way of life). Why 5S matters Reduces non-value-added activities and waste (time searching, motion, inventory). Improves safety, morale, and quality; makes school/factory/office conditions problems visible at a glance. Creates the foundation for other lean methods (TPM, just-in-time, Six Sigma, Kaizen). Improves customers' first impressions of a workplace. Variations Some practitioners add a sixth S: Safety (establish and practice safety procedures). Toyota traditionally uses just 4S (Seiton and Seiso combined; audits replace Shitsuke) — but now uses 5S as standard. Two main frameworks: Osada and Hirano (Hirano structured 5S as sequential improvement steps). Although it originated in manufacturing, 5S also applies to offices, warehouses, workstations, and even knowledge work (information/software in place of physical product). Sources US EPA – Lean Thinking and Methods: 5S (epa.gov/sustainability) Lean Enterprise Institute – 5S lexicon entry (lean.org) ASQ – 5S of Lean tutorial (asq.org) Wikipedia – 5S (methodology) Images: Wikimedia Commons – Category:5S

h: Brief History of BPO Sector in the Philippines
A Glimpse Into the Past, Present, and Future of the BPO Industry in the Philippines
pages.b: One of the most robust sectors in the Philippines right now is the information technology and business process outsourcing (IT-BPO) sector. More than just a lucrative enterprise, the IT-BPO sector has also proven to be the largest and fastest-growing industry in the country. There is no denying its major role in providing quality jobs and encouraging economic activity and investment even in areas outside Metro Manila. Of course, the IT-BPO industry was not an overnight affair. Credit is due to the handful of individuals who saw the potential in the business in its early stages. Among them are the likes of Rainier "Bong" Borja, who is often regarded as the most articulate voice of the Philippine BPO industry; Karen Batungbacal for her early involvement and series of contact center firms; and Secretary Mar Roxas, who, during his tenure as secretary of the Department of Trade and Industry, saw the potential of the industry, reached out to key leaders to promote foreign investment, and helped shape the landscape of BPO into what it is today. Brief History of BPO Sector in the Philippines Timeline Highlights 1992 — First Contact Center: Frank Holz, under the Accenture group, created the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995 — Special Economic Zone Act: The Philippine Congress passed this act, lowering area requirements for development and offering tax incentives to attract foreign investors. 1997 — First BPO Multinational: Sykes Asia established operations, becoming the first multinational BPO company in the Philippines. 1999 — First Call Center: Jim Franke and Derek Holley founded eTelecare, which became widely recognized as the country's first call center. 2000 — GDP Contribution: The BPO industry accounted for 0.075% of the Philippines' total GDP. 2001 — Expansion & Job Creation: PeopleSupport, a US-based outsourcing center, restructured its business operations to move to the Philippines, generating approximately 8,400 jobs. 2003 — Convergys Expansion: Convergys Corp. opened two call centers in the country. Chosen alongside India by company president Jack Freker, this formed a key part of their global growth plan. 2005 — Global Market Share: The Philippines captured 3% of the global BPO market, which represented 2.4% of the country's GDP. 2006 — PLDT Ventus & Growth: PLDT Ventus emerged at the forefront of the local BPO landscape, helping boost the Philippine domestic economy by 5.4%. Around 11,000 individuals were employed across North America, Europe, and Asia. 2010 — BPO Capital Title: The Philippines earned the recognition of being the "world's BPO capital", employing over 525,000 people in call centers and generating $8.9 billion in revenue. 2011 — Top Job Provider: The sector became one of the fastest-growing job providers in the private sector, generating $11 billion in revenue, employing 638,000 Filipinos, and comprising 4.9% of total GDP. 2012 — Continued Expansion: Industry revenues reached 5.4% of total GDP, maintaining a growth rate of around 46% annually since 2006. 2013 — Milestone Numbers: Revenue climbed to $15.5 billion, with full-time employment reaching 900,000 Filipinos. 2016 — Long-Term Projection: Projections estimated the industry would generate 1.3 million new jobs with a 17% annual growth rate. A Glimpse Into the Past, Present, and Future of the BPO Industry in the Philippines Timeline 1992: Accenture establishes the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995: The Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) is established. 1999: eTelecare, the first call center company in the country, is founded. 2000: The BPO sector contributes 0.075% to the Philippine GDP. 2001: Establishment of the Contact Center Association of the Philippines (CCAP). 2002: Proposal to revise Republic Act 7916 to extend tax perks to PEZA-registered BPOs. 2005: The BPO industry captures 3% of the global market. 2006: The BPO sector experiences a 46% annual growth rate. 2008: The Philippines surpasses India in BPO growth. 2010: The Philippines officially earns the title of the BPO capital of the world. 2019: The BPO industry thrives despite pandemic-related shutdowns. 2020: According to PEZA, IT-BPO investment pledges increased by 37% from January to July 2020. 2021: The outsourcing industry continues to grow despite the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. 2022: IBPAP actively lobbies for the permanent adoption of hybrid work. 2023: The country boasts more than 700 BPO companies. 2024: More than 850 BPO companies. 2028: 59 billion target revenue. 2030: AI roadmap estimated a $92 billion GDP contribution by 2030. deadline: jul 23, 12:00PM 2026 On your notebook, write the appropriate meaning and roles of the following terminologies in Philippine BPO: GCC PSIA GDAP CCAP HIMAP GICC ACPI IBPAP IT-BMP SLA NDA SMP BPS TAT HR VA OM TSR SEO CSR with your name and class section hand written perpendicularly along the side of the page. Take photo of such notes then post/save the same on or before 12 noon july 23 This cluster of acronyms heavily represents the IT & Business Process Management (IT-BPM) sector, global shared services, and standard business operations. Industry Associations & Governing Bodies IBPAP – IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines The primary umbrella association and trade organization for the IT-BPM sector in the Philippines, working with government and academia to drive industry growth. PSIA – Philippine Software Industry Association An industry association representing software development, tech solutions, and IT service companies. GDAP – Game Developers Association of the Philippines The organization representing local game design, interactive media, and digital entertainment studios. CCAP – Contact Center Association of the Philippines The trade association representing contact centers, call centers, and customer experience operations. HIMAP – Healthcare Information Management Association of the Philippines An association representing companies providing health IT, medical coding, transcription, and healthcare BPO services. GICC – Global In-House Center Council The industry association representing captive corporate shared service centers and global capability centers.akoa ACPI – Animation Council of the Philippines, Inc. The trade group representing animation studios, 2D/3D visual artists, and post-production service providers. Business Models, Sectors & Programs GCC – Global Capability Center (Primary IT-BPM Context) An in-house, offshore/nearshore facility established by a global company to perform core operations, engineering, IT, or analytics tasks internally. (Alternative Macroeconomic Context: Gulf Cooperation Council ) IT-BMP / IT-BPM – Information Technology and Business Process Management The overarching business sector that delivers technology services, back-office operations, and customer support via outsourcing or shared services. (Also referred to as IT-BMP for IT-Business Management Program/Process). BPS – Business Process Services Outsourced operational tasks and functions (e.g., HR, accounting, customer care) managed by an external provider or internal shared service team. SMP – Service Management Program (IT-BPM Context) An industry-designed academic track integrated into university curricula to prepare students for management and operational roles in the IT-BPM sector. (Alternative Marketing Context: Social Media Platform / Social Media Plan ) Legal, Service Standards & Metrics SLA – Service Level Agreement A formal contract defining specific service performance standards (e.g., response time, resolution rate, system uptime) between a service provider and client. NDA – Non-Disclosure Agreement A legal contract designed to protect confidential business details, client data, and proprietary trade secrets from unauthorized disclosure. TAT – Turnaround Time The total elapsed time required to process, complete, and deliver a task or request from start to finish. Operational Roles & Functional Units HR – Human Resources The business unit handling recruitment, payroll, employee management, training, and corporate policy. VA – Virtual Assistant A remote administrative or specialist contractor providing virtual support to a business or individual. (Also refers to Voice Analytics in contact center tech). OM – Operations Manager A managerial role overseeing daily team workflows, delivery quality, efficiency, and operational execution. TSR – Technical Support Representative A frontline customer service specialist trained to troubleshoot technical, network, hardware, or software issues. CSR – Customer Service Representative / Corporate Social Responsibility Operations Role: Customer Service Representative – A agent handling customer inquiries, orders, and issue resolution. Corporate Governance: Corporate Social Responsibility – Business practices intended to make a positive impact on society and the environment. SEO – Search Engine Optimization Digital marketing techniques aimed at improving website content visibility and ranking on search engine result pages. files: https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/1wMf-X987BxQc10EKSYGFQxWHzOndkrbs

CompAInion Rules Standing instructions for the CompAInion AI copilot. They are loaded into the assistant's instructions on every message. Edit this note freely - changes apply from your next message. Remove rules you do not want and add your own under any heading. If this note is missing, CompAInion recreates it with these defaults the next time the plugin loads. Quizzes and self-testing When asked to build a quiz from your notes, build a self-test, not an answer sheet: The quiz must NOT contain any answers. The user fills in the answer fields themselves. Number the questions (1., 2., ...). Quiz content must come from the notes you read, never from general knowledge. Put every question in its own callout, exactly in this shape: 1. Which template engine does Symfony use? A. Blade B. Twig C. Vue D. Mustache Answer: Copy Multiple choice: exactly four checkbox options (A-D) inside the same callout. True/False: - [ ] True and - [ ] False checkboxes inside the callout. Identification (short answer): no options; the numbered question plus the empty answer field only. Leave every answer field empty while creating or updating a quiz, and never pre-fill options as correct. This no-answers rule protects quiz creation. A quiz note may end with the line: "Ask the AI to evaluate your answers when you're done." When the user asks you to evaluate, grade, or check their answers, do it by GRADING THE NOTE, not in chat: Read the quiz note and the source notes it was built from. Judge only from the user's checked boxes and typed answer fields. Rewrite the quiz note with ONE update operation. Keep every question, its wording, and the user's checked boxes exactly as they are; only add verdicts. Add one score callout at the very top, above the first question: > [!success] Score: 15/20 - 75% . Add one verdict callout directly after each answered question, as its own block quote. Correct answers are shown on purpose during grading: right answer: > [!check] 1. Correct - enable (green) wrong answer: > [!fail] 6. Wrong - you picked VLAN 100 STAFF; correct is VLAN 200 FACULTY, because PC0's access port is in VLAN 200 in the Basic Setup lab. (red) A multiple choice or True/False question with no checked option is wrong; with more than one checked option is wrong. An identification question with an empty answer field is wrong. Keep the chat_reply brief: just the score and that the note now contains the full grading. General Put new quiz and study notes into the same folder as their source notes unless told otherwise. Keep answers factual and sourced from the vault notes you read. The creator of the CompAInion plugin is nataho.

Challenge 1 Feature / Category Male Reproductive System Female Reproductive System Similarities and Differences Primary Sex Characteristics & Gonads - Gonads are the testes . - Produce sperm (germ cells) and testosterone (androgen). - Gonads are the ovaries . - House ova/eggs (germ cells) and produce estrogen and progesterone . - Similarity: Both use primary sex organs (gonads) present at birth to make germ cells and sex hormones. - Goal: Both work together to produce offspring and create new life. External Genitalia (Outer Hardware) - External organs are the penis (head, shaft, root), scrotum, prepuce (foreskin), corona, frenulum, urethral opening, and perineum.ng the glans penis. - External organs form the vulva (mons veneris, labia majora and minora, prepuce, vestibule, clitoris, openings, and perineum). - Similarity: Both have external sex organs (genitals) present at birth. Both have a prepuce (clitoral hood or penis foreskin). - Difference: The perineum space between the genitals and anus is longer in males than in females. Internal Parts & Pathways (Inner Hardware) - Includes testes, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts, prostate gland, and urethra. - Seminal vesicles (70%) and prostate (30%) produce alkaline fluid to feed sperm and protect them from acid. - Includes ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus (womb), cervix, and vagina. - Fallopian tubes carry eggs to the uterus; the vagina is a collapsible canal that engorges during arousal. - Similarity: Both have inner organs and tubes to carry germ cells. - Difference: The male urethra carries both urine and semen out of the body. In females, the urethral opening (urine) and vaginal opening are separate. Germ Cell Output - Produces sperm in virtually unlimited amounts over a lifespan. - Born with ~1 million immature ova, but only 400–450 mature in a lifetime. - Difference: Males make a continuous, unlimited supply of sperm, while females are born with a set number of eggs that stop maturing around age 45–50 (menopause). Hormones & Cycles - Driven mainly by testosterone from the testes. - Has no monthly cycle. - Driven by estrogen and progesterone from the ovaries. - Governed by the hypothalamus in a monthly cycle lasting 24 to 42 days. - Difference: Females experience a monthly cycle with menstrual bleeding when an egg is unfertilized. Males do not have a monthly cycle. Secondary Sex Characteristics (Puberty Changes) - Broader shoulders and deeper chest. - Voice breaks/deepens. - Taller with more body/facial hair and higher body water. - Breast enlargement (glandular and fatty tissue). - Widening of hips and pelvis. - Generally shorter with a higher proportion of body fat. - Similarity: Both develop secondary sex characteristics during puberty when gonads ramp up hormone production. - Difference: Males build broader shoulders and deeper voices, while females develop breasts and wider hips. Challenge 2 Stage 1: Birth (Primary Characteristics) Female Specs External genitals (vulva, labia, clitoris) present Shorter Distance between genitals and anus Ovaries house around 1 million immature ova Male Specs External genitals (penis, scrotum, foreskin) present Greater distance between genitals and anus Stage 2: Childhood Both Sexes Physical and emotional changes toward adulthood Female Immature ova remain dominant in ovaries Stage 3: Puberty (system update) Female Changes Breasts form Hips and pelvis widen First period (menarche) at ages 11 to 15 Monthly cycle begins via hypothalamus Male Changes Genitals develop Pubic and body hair grows Voice breaks and deepens Growth spurt with broader shoulders Testosterone drives sperm creation Stage 4: Adulthood and aging Female path Only 400 to 450 ova mature across the lifespan Monthly Cycle lasts 24 to 42 days Menopause occurs around ages 45 to 50 Two X chromosomes lead to longer lifespan Male Path Unlimited sperm production over lifespan No monthly cycle Facial hair and increased baldness risk Single X Chromosome increases colorblindness risk

SOGIE & GAD Interview Report Interviewee: Hon. Virginia G. Ong Age: 48 Position: Sangguniang Bayan (SB) Member, Sindangan, Zamboanga del Norte Length of Service: 1st term Interview Responses GAD Policies Awareness: Guided by CEDAW and the Magna Carta of Women (RA 9710), ensuring the mandatory 5% GAD budget allocation Yes. Internationally, there is the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW). Locally, our municipality is strictly guided by the Magna Carta of Women (Republic Act No. 9710) and the mandatory 5% GAD budget allocation for local government units. Proposed GAD Ordinances: Co-sponsored resolutions for the annual GAD Plan (funding maternal health, VAWC desks, and local livelihood). As part of the municipal council, I regularly co-sponsor the resolutions approving our annual GAD Plan and Budget. This ensures our local funds are explicitly directed toward maternal health services, the maintenance of VAWC (Violence Against Women and their Children) desks across our barangays, and local livelihood training. Spearheaded Programs: Backed National Women's Month initiatives and livelihood seminars for mothers in coastal/agricultural communities. I actively support our local National Women's Month initiatives every March and help spearhead community-level livelihood seminars. These activities aim to provide financial independence and skills training for mothers in our coastal and agricultural communities here in Sindangan. SOGIE Discrimination Cases: Addressed subtle community discrimination by mediating issues alongside local barangay captains. While Sindanganons are naturally welcoming, subtle discrimination occasionally happens in workplaces or community spaces. When informal complaints reach my office, I coordinate with the respective barangay captains to mediate the issue and ensure the individuals involved are treated with dignity and fairness. Future SOGIE Ordinance: Planning to draft a local Anti-Discrimination Ordinance penalizing SOGIE-based prejudice in employment, education, and municipal services. Yes. Drafting a comprehensive local Anti-Discrimination Ordinance is a goal of mine. The basic content would prohibit and penalize discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, and expression (SOGIE) in local employment, educational institutions, and the delivery of municipal public services. Future SOGIE Programs: Proposing SOGIE sensitivity and awareness seminars specifically for municipal frontliners, local police, and barangay officials. Absolutely. I plan to propose SOGIE sensitivity and awareness seminars specifically tailored for our municipal frontliners, local police, and barangay officials. This will ensure that when LGBTQ+ constituents seek public assistance, they are met with understanding rather than prejudice. pages.b: Unpacking the Human Experience: A Modern Exploration of Biology, Society, and Self Lesson Roadmap & Learning Objectives Differentiate between biological sex, gender, and sexual orientation. Understand the social, cultural, and psychological implications of these differences. Reflect on personal identity and the importance of fostering an inclusive, diverse environment. 1. Defining the Core Triad Human experience is shaped by three interconnected yet distinct dimensions: Sex: The biological aspects of maleness or femaleness (chromosomes, anatomy, hormones). Gender: The social interpretation of sex (masculinity, femininity, cultural expectations). Sexuality: The totality of an individual's personal experience regarding their sex and gender. 2. The 4-Layer Framework of Human Identity Layer 1: Biological Sex ("The Hardware / The Body") Biological sex is the biological dimension determined by reproductive anatomy and genetic markers. It is typically assigned at birth based on external physical characteristics. Components of Sex Biology: Chromosomes: Genetic structures (XX typically denotes female; XY typically denotes male). Hormones: Chemical drivers (females generally have higher levels of estrogen/progesterone; males have higher testosterone). Anatomy: Internal reproductive organs and external genitalia. The Intersex Spectrum: Biological sex is not strictly binary. Intersex refers to individuals born with chromosomal variations or composite genital characteristics combining male and female traits. Occurs in approximately 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). Replaces the historical term hermaphroditism . Layer 2: Gender & Society ("The Software / Socialization") Gender is a social construct. Because humans are "meaning-making organisms," higher-order thinking leads societies to assign cultural meaning to biological sex. The Socialization Timeline: Birth: Immediate assignment of gendered expectations (e.g., blue for boyhood, pink for girlhood). Childhood: Family members select toys, clothes, and activities based on interpreted sex. Adolescence: Rules expand into strict social and behavioral expectations. Adulthood: Norms influence career paths, fields of study, and societal roles. Heteronormativity: The assumption or societal standard that judges behavior as "normal" only when it strictly conforms to traditional expectations associated with biological sex (e.g., expecting girls to be gentle/caring and boys to be strong/assertive). Evolving Social Norms: Gender expression standards change over time. For example, 60 years ago, women wearing pants faced heavy social disapproval, whereas today it is standard fashion. Rejection of traditional gender roles (e.g., boys rejecting rough sports or girls rejecting dresses) represents natural variations in human expression. Layer 3: Gender Identity ("The Internal Compass / The Mind") Gender identity is an internal, deeply felt sense of who one is—experiencing oneself as a man, a woman, non-binary, or another identity. Cisgender: Individual whose internal gender identity aligns with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender: Individual whose internal gender identity does not align with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender Woman: Assigned male at birth; identifies as a woman. Transgender Man: Assigned female at birth; identifies as a man. Note on Medical Transition: Some transgender individuals choose gender reassignment processes to align physical traits with identity, while others do not due to personal beliefs, cultural context, or economic factors. Layer 4: Sexual Orientation ("The Heart / Attraction") Sexual orientation describes the pattern of emotional, romantic, and sexual attraction toward others. Developmental Timeline: Emotional and sexual attraction typically begins developing around ages 6 to 8 (Psychological Association of the Philippines - PAP). Dating and relationship experimentation generally occurs during adolescence. Key Definitions: Heterosexual (Straight): Attraction to individuals of the opposite sex/gender. Homosexual (Gay/Lesbian): Attraction to individuals of the same sex/gender. Bisexual: Attraction to individuals of both male and female sexes/genders. LGBT: An acronym representing the Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender community. 3. Synthesis: The Identity Matrix ("Identity Sliders") Human identity is not a simple binary switch. Instead, it operates on four independent, continuously variable axes : Axis Category Spectrum / Extremes Biological Sex The Body Female ↔ Intersex ↔ Male Gender Expression Society / Visual Feminine ↔ Androgynous ↔ Masculine Gender Identity The Mind Woman ↔ Non-binary ↔ Man Sexual Orientation The Heart Attracted to Men ↔ Both/All ↔ Attracted to Women Key Takeaway: Every human being represents a unique, custom configuration across these four independent sliders. 4. Psychological Safety & Inclusivity Personal Discovery: Sexual orientation and gender identity are deeply personal internal processes. A person's identity can only truly be known if they choose to share their lived experiences and feelings. Impact of Prejudice: Individuals subjected to discrimination, stigma, or prejudice suffer negative psychological effects. Goal: Creating safe, inclusive, and empathetic environments enables everyone to express their authentic selves without fear of harm or social isolation. Self-Test Knowledge Check What term describes biological markers such as XX/XY chromosomes? Answer: Biological Sex. How frequently do intersex traits occur in births? Answer: Roughly 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). What term describes someone whose internal gender identity differs from their assigned sex at birth? Answer: Transgender. At what age range does attraction typically begin developing according to the PAP? Answer: Ages 6 to 8.

PHP talking to a database — the part that makes a website actually work . get data from the user, validate it, clean it, then save it to the database through PDO. that's basically every account system ever built. Getting data from the user php grabs submitted form data through two built-ins — the difference is how it travels, not whether you can use it: $_GET — data rides along in the URL ( ?name=Owen ). visible in the address bar, bookmark-able. fine for searches and filters, never for passwords. $_POST — data travels hidden inside the request body. this is the one for logins, form submissions, saving stuff. html Copy <!-- form jumps into $_GET --> < form method = "get" action = "search.php" > < input name = "query" > < button > Search </ button > </ form > <!-- form jumps into $_POST --> < form method = "post" action = "signup.php" > < input type = "password" name = "password" > < button > Sign Up </ button > </ form > php Copy $name = $_POST [ 'name' ]; // one array per method $pass = $_POST [ 'password' ]; Core validation techniques the four checks every field should get: required — empty? reject. trim() + empty() are the tools here type/format — an email has to actually look like an email length/range — time to enforce a minimum, a maximum, or range pattern — regex for the weird formats (phone numbers, student IDs) php Copy // 1. required — reject empty if ( empty ( trim ( $_POST [ 'name' ]))) { $errors [] = "Name is required" ; } // 2. type/format if (! filter_var ( $_POST [ 'email' ], FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) { $errors [] = "That email looks fake" ; } // 3. length/range if ( strlen ( $_POST [ 'name' ]) < 2 || strlen ( $_POST [ 'name' ]) > 50 ) { $errors [] = "Name must be 2–50 characters" ; } // 4. pattern — digits only if (! preg_match ( '/^[0-9]+$/' , $_POST [ 'phone' ])) { $errors [] = "Phone must be digits only" ; } Sanitation and filter functions validate decides if a value is acceptable . sanitize cleans it up. a good form does both. plus htmlspecialchars() before printing user input back onto a page so nobody injects HTML at your users. Great helpers to know: trim() — strips whitespace from both ends htmlspecialchars() — converts special chars safely, for when you print input back out (a note in the server-side armor against XSS) strip_tags() — removes tags entirely filter_var() — validate or sanitize in one shot, just tell it what you're checking php Copy $dirty = " user@example.com " ; $email = trim ( $dirty ); // 1. trim the edges $email = filter_var ( $email , FILTER_SANITIZE_EMAIL); // 2. clean it if ( filter_var ( $email , FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) { // 3. now check it // good to go } // when you print it back out on a page: echo htmlspecialchars ( $name , ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8' ); Connecting with PDO PDO = PHP Data Objects — the standard way for PHP to talk to a database. set it up like this: create a database folder (yes, folder literally named database in your project) inside it, create a config.php the four variables every connection needs: variable means $host ip of the host ( 127.0.0.1 while developing on your machine) $db the database name $user username of the host-account $password the host account's password database/config.php : php Copy <?php $host = "127.0.0.1" ; $db = "webdev-db" ; $user = "root" ; $password = "root" ; // DSN — one string that says: server, database, charset $dsn = "mysql:host= $host ;dbname= $db ;charset=utf8mb4" ; $pdo = new PDO ( $dsn , $user , $password ); // shout at me when something breaks — exceptions over silence $pdo -> setAttribute (PDO:: ATTR_ERRMODE , PDO:: ERRMODE_EXCEPTION ); ?> what's happening: the DSN (Data Source Name) is the connection address built in one string: mysql:host=...;dbname=...;charset=... charset=utf8mb4 — so emojis and weird characters don't crash your queries ERRMODE_EXCEPTION — PDO fails loudly with exceptions instead of shutting up, which makes debugging way easier use it from any page: php Copy require 'database/config.php' ; $stmt = $pdo -> query ( "SELECT * FROM products" ); $products = $stmt -> fetchAll (); foreach ( $products as $row ) { echo htmlspecialchars ( $row [ 'name' ]); } heads up two different config.php files exist in this course and they do different jobs: this one (in database/ ) handles the database connection , while the one from Personal Techniques handles .urls and paths . both at the same time. i know. it confused me for a bit too lmao See also Personal Techniques — reusing the html around your php cleanly Docker — running MySQL/‌phpMyAdmin in containers instead of installing locally Midterm Website — where all of this actually gets used Symfony — the framework that wraps a lot of this for you

JavaScript is what turns a static page into an actually interactive one — reading, changing, creating, and removing page content, and reacting to whatever the user does. and the best part: all of that happens live, in the browser, with zero page reloads. Client-Side vs Server-Side quick before anything else — "client side" just means it runs in the user's browser , not on the server. Client-Side Server-Side runs on the user's browser the web server language JavaScript PHP (and its friends) what triggers it clicks, typing, scrolling HTTP requests speed instant, no reload whatever the network gives you access only what's already in the page databases, server files, secrets typical use form validation, UI, animations login, saving to the database the three pillars, in one line each: HTML — the structure CSS — the looks JavaScript — the behavior The DOM when the browser loads your HTML, it doesn't keep the file as-is. it turns every single tag into an object and arranges them into a tree. that tree is the DOM — the Document Object Model. it's a live version of your page that JavaScript can touch, and when you change the DOM, the screen updates instantly. css variables store a value once and reuse it everywhere. define them with --name , drop them in with var(--name) . change the variable once, and every place using it updates with it. global variables are declared inside :root (the document's root element) local ones can be declared inside any other selector the name must begin with -- css Copy :root { --primary-color : red; } h1 { color : var (--primary-color); } the real thing, from my site below is the actual palette and header styling from my website — every color lives in a variable up top, so a re-theme means changing four lines, not forty. css Copy @import url( 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fontsource/adwaita-mono@5.0.0/index.css' ); } body { background-color : var (--palette-darker); font-family : 'Adwaita Mono' , monospace; margin : 0 ; padding : 20px ; } header { background-color : var (--transparent-darker); border-radius : 20px ; padding : 40px ; display : flex; flex-direction : row; justify-content : space-between; align-items : center; gap : 20px ; } nav { font-family : inherit; margin-top : 20px ; } p { color : var (--palette-lighter); } h1 { font-size : 2.5em ; color : var (--palette-light); margin : 0 ; } .heading-text { flex : 1 ; } .heading-nav { background-color : var (--palette-dark); font-size : 20px ; padding : 10px 20px ; display : inline-block; text-decoration : none; border-radius : 20px ; color : var (--palette-darker); transition : background-color 0.2s ease; /* Smooth hover transition */ } .heading-nav :hover { background-color : var (--palette-light); } .heading-img { width : 250px ; height : auto; object-fit : cover; /* Keeps image from stretching */ flex-shrink : 0 ; border-radius : 10px ; -webkit- mask-image : linear-gradient (to right, transparent 0% , black 40% ); mask-image : linear-gradient (to right, transparent 0% , black 40% ); } what to look at: the --palette-* names keep the four shades sorted from darker → lighter, so you don't have to remember the hexes --transparent-darker is a hex with an alpha channel — 3F = 25% transparent black mask-image fades the right edge of the header image out with a gradient, so it blends into the background instead of ending as a hard box .heading-nav:hover — the hover part is a pseudo class ; the transition makes the swap smooth See also CSS3 and CSS Frameworks — the master css note this belongs to Pseudo classes — the :hover used above Measurement Units — the 2.5em , 250px and friends used above

the css master note — what css is, how syntax works, and where every html element gets styled with it. css is a language used to specify the formatting of an html document. html gives the page its structure, css decides what everything looks like. CSS syntax a css rule is built out of four pieces: selector — which element(s) to target: h1 , h2 , p , div , .btn , #title declaration block — the { } that holds your declarations property — what you're changing ( color , font-size , etc.) value — what you're changing it to ( color: blue ) css Copy h1 { color : blue; font-size : 12px ; } types of selectors how you grab the element(s) to style — by id, class, tag, attribute, or all of them at once. covered in detail in types of selectors . Embedding a style external style definitions live on their own file, embedded into the html document with the link tag. html Copy < link rel = "stylesheet" href = "file/loc" > internal html Copy < head > < style > .classname {} </ style > </ head > inline html Copy < h2 style = "color:red;" > </ h2 > the cascade when more than one style targets the same element, the cascade decides who wins. priority order: inline internal external browser defaults CSS variables the var() function is used to insert the value of a css variable css variables can have a global or local scope to create a global variable, declare it inside the :root selector — :root matches the document's root element a css variable name must begin with -- css Copy :root { --primary-color : red; } h1 { color : var (--primary-color); } full notes in CSS variables , including a real palette from my own site. Measurement Units the units of measurement used in css. the slide table is in Measurement Units . CSS box model a box that wraps around every html element — content, padding, border, margin. CSS background properties background properties of elements. CSS transforms to do add the css transforms table from the lecture. CSS transitions to do add the css transition properties. CSS transitions is still a stub. CSS animation there's a proper css animation route too, but doing it the manual way is not advisable — you place every movement by hand instead of letting keyframes do the in-betweens. Pseudo classes used to define a state of an element — hover, active, focus and friends. detail and examples in Pseudo classes . css Copy selector:pseudo-class { color : white; } h2 :first-child { color : red; } viewport the viewport tag tells a mobile browser to treat the screen width as the actual width, instead of pretending it's a desktop and zooming out. responsive styling ( media queries ) depends on it. html Copy < meta name = "viewport" content = "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" > media types all — used for all media types and devices print — used for printers screen — used for computer screens, tablets, smartphones speech — used for screen readers that "read" the page out loud syntax: css Copy @media [media type] and ( min-width ) and ( max-width ) { } css Copy @media screen and ( min-width : 400px ) { } the full guide lives in media types . CSS frameworks bootstrap 5 (component-first) gives you pre-built components out of the box used for prototyping and generic websites tailwind css 4.3 (utility-first) used for complex and customizable elements and components See also Client-Side Scripting — the javascript that hooks into everything above php and database — what happens on the other side of the form Pseudo classes — element states, where hover lives

pages.b: What is Docker? docker is an app that makes migrating systems, servers, databases, etc. a lot easier. the way docker does it is with images and containers . just let the next machine install docker only , and it's ready to migrate! What if we don't use docker? if you don't use docker when migrating, the system might break. it could be because of: outdated / unstable software, no prerequisite packages, inconsistent configuration, and more. Images images are one of the key features of docker. images are packages that are ready to be copied and deployed to your container so it can be used immediately. Analogy think of an image as a photo of a document. you can still read the document right? but you can't edit it, just scan it. once the image has been scanned, it can then be edited again and be used again. in plainer terms: the image is the frozen package — you don't touch it yourself. you run it, and what's running it is the container. one image can spawn as many copies of a container as you want. Containers containers are also one of the key features of docker. containers are basically tiny virtual machines with their own apps and services running — and those services would be your running images. Setting up docker Images needed mysql php Create network bash Copy docker network create [name of network] Example bash Copy docker network create webdev-network most basic command to create a container DISCLAIMER NOT RECOMMENDED TO RUN THIS BY ITSELF bash Copy docker run -d [name of container] why it's not recommended a bare run like this has no network, no volume, no environment variables, nothing. the full versions below include all of those — use those instead. command to find if a port is used (windows) bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr [portnumber] Example bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr 3306 if something is using port 3306 , you get output like this. if the port is free, the command just prints nothing. Copy TCP 0.0.0.0:3306 0.0.0.0:0 LISTENING 18196 TCP [::]:3306 [::]:0 LISTENING 18196 Creating containers this is where containers actually get created. the templates here take the full docker run from earlier and add the network, volume, environment variables, and port mapping you'll actually need in class. MySQL container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -v [Volume Name]:[Volume Location] -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=[Mysql Password] -e MYSQL_DATABASE=[DatabaseName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-mysql --network webdev-network -v webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=webdev-db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 phpMyAdmin container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -e PMA_HOST=[MysqlContainerName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-phpmyadmin --network webdev-network -e PMA_HOST=webdev-mysql -p 3311:80 phpmyadmin My command DISCLAIMER DO NOT COPY THIS. THIS COMMAND IS IRRELEVANT TO YOUR PROJECTS bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_mysql --network EB_Network -v EB-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=EB_shop -p 6967:3306 mysql:8.0 bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_phpmyadmin --network EB_Network -e PMA_HOST=EB_mysql -p 6969:80 phpmyadmin Extra docker commands from the notes of Sir Ariel Bensing. Build an image from a dockerfile bash Copy docker build -t symfony-app . the . at the end matters — it points to the dockerfile in the current folder . Build the container based on the image bash Copy docker run --name symfony-app-demo --network platform-network -p 8000:8000 symfony-app Create a network bash Copy docker network create platform-network Build a container for MySQL bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-db --network platform-network -v symfony-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=app_db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 Build a container for phpMyAdmin bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-pma --network platform-network -p 8081:80 -e PMA_HOST=symfony-db phpmyadmin Execute a command inside a running container bash Copy docker exec -it symfony-app-demo "symfony command" Inspect a network bash Copy docker network inspect [network name] Delete a network bash Copy docker network rm [network name] Delete a container bash Copy docker rm [container name] Delete an image bash Copy docker rmi [image name] Stop a container bash Copy docker stop [container name] took me a while to realize stop is for containers, not networks lmao. networks don't stop, they just exist until you rm them. Extra on symfony to connect to your database you have to open your .env file on the root folder. Making variables env Copy MYSQL_USER= MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP= MYSQL_PORT= MYSQL_DATABASE= Example my database has these variables to connect to. it doesn't mean you can copy this and make it work on yours — you have to provide your own values. env Copy MYSQL_USER=root MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP=127.0.0.1 MYSQL_PORT=3306 MYSQL_DATABASE=eb_shop Connecting to database using the variables from #Making variables to connect to the database: env Copy DATABASE_URL="mysql://${MYSQL_USER}:${MYSQL_PASSWORD}@${MYSQL_IP}:${MYSQL_PORT}/${MYSQL_DATABASE}?serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB&charset=utf8mb4" you can copy this one if you want. drop database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:drop --force create database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:create Using compose.yaml spelling the file is named compose.yaml — compose , not composer . composer is the PHP package thing, easy to mix up. both files exist in a symfony project and they do totally different jobs. using compose.yaml is one of the great things of Symfony and docker. it allows you to create containers when needed and delete them when not used or powered off. it also allows you to migrate your project easily, because the whole setup is stored in the project itself and not inside a separate database. it's all in one file. IMPORTANT change your compose.override.yaml to compose.override-disabled.yaml or basically delete it so that it doesn't interfere with your development. Editing compose.yaml everything inside this file is the same thing the manual docker run commands did earlier. what this basically does is create 2 containers named webdev-mysql and webdev-phpmyadmin , and their images are in the name. yaml Copy services: webdev-mysql: image: mysql:8.0 container_name: webdev-mysql restart: unless-stopped environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD} MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE} MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER} MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD} ports: - "6666:3306" volumes: - webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql networks: - webdev-network webdev-phpmyadmin: image: phpmyadmin container_name: webdev-phpmyadmin restart: unless-stopped environment: PMA_HOST: webdev-mysql ports: - "7777:80" networks: - webdev-network volumes: webdev-db-data: networks: webdev-network: this file is also connected to the .env file — that's why you see those ${MYSQL_DATABASE} things. Essential commands for compose to work DISCLAIMER the following commands WILL NOT WORK if the terminal you are using is NOT inside the root folder of your project. start the containers bash Copy docker compose up -d stop the containers bash Copy docker compose stop stop them and remove everything (containers + volumes) bash Copy docker compose down -v How to create an entity entities are tables inside the database. (this part is still a work in progress, to be filled in properly after more discussions.) bash Copy symfony console make:entity Category bash Copy symfony console make:migration bash Copy symfony console doctrine:migrations:migrate bash Copy symfony console make:crud Category How to connect 2 tables when making the second entity ( Product ), the prompt asks what it is related to — these are the answers to hit: bash Copy symfony console make:entity Product category <- field name ManyToOne <- the relation Category <- the other entity no <- store the whole object? yes <- is it nullable? symfony console make:migration symfony console doctrine:migrations:migrate symfony console make:crud Product See also php and database — the mysql side these containers run Symfony — the framework that talks to the database this sets up Midterm Website — where all of this gets used for real

Related: Symfony and Docker Context source database : eb_shop on XAMPP MariaDB 10.4.32 ( 127.0.0.1:3306 , user root , no password) target : Docker compose stack in the format from Docker — eb-mysql (MySQL 8.0) + eb-phpmyadmin — kept blank ; data gets entered by me, not the AI project : C:\Users\Nataho\Documents\school\webdev\symfony\finals — Symfony 8.1, PHP 8.4, Doctrine 3, maker-bundle present work split: I run every command , the AI writes the code . the tables below tell me what to type at every prompt. 6967/6969 are free; remove stale manual EB_* containers if still around 4. update .env — adds MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD , app user, port 6967 , serverVersion 5. docker compose up -d → verify both containers Up + phpMyAdmin alive at :6969 6. check Symfony can reach the DB ( dbal:run-sql ) 7. make:entity × 4 → Product, Order, OrderItem, Image (User already exists) 8. pin table/PK/FK names on all entities ships in the stack now) run everything from the project root: bash Copy cd "C:\Users\Nataho\Documents\school\webdev\symfony\finals" Step 1 — compose.yaml in the professor's format the Symfony recipe's compose.yaml runs PostgreSQL 16 with a random exposed port, and a compose.override.yaml stacks on top of it — none of that matches the format from Docker : two containers (MySQL + phpMyAdmin), explicit container_name s, one named network, one named volume, ports fixed at sensible numbers. swap both files out. 1a — disable the override IMPORTANT — from the notes change your compose.override.yaml to compose.override-disabled.yaml or basically delete it so that it doesn't interfere with your development. bash Copy Rename-Item compose.override.yaml compose.override-disabled.yaml side effect: Mailpit leaves the stack the override was the only thing running Mailpit. fine for the shop — .env has MAILER_DSN=null://null anyway. 1b — replace compose.yaml replace the entire contents of compose.yaml with this (same shape as Docker § Using compose.yaml : it creates two containers named eb-mysql and eb-phpmyadmin , images in the name): yaml Copy services: eb-mysql: image: mysql:8.0 container_name: eb-mysql restart: unless-stopped environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD} MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE} MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER} MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD} ports: - "6967:3306" volumes: - eb-db-data:/var/lib/mysql networks: - eb-network eb-phpmyadmin: image: phpmyadmin container_name: eb-phpmyadmin restart: unless-stopped environment: PMA_HOST: eb-mysql ports: - "6969:80" networks: - eb-network volumes: eb-db-data: networks: eb-network: those ${...} placeholders are read straight from the project's .env — that's the whole trick from the notes. the old recipe also left behind a volume called database_data (PostgreSQL data files); nothing references it now, so it just sits unused — leave it, or clean it: docker compose down then docker volume rm finals_database_data . 1c — before up : check ports + stale containers XAMPP's MariaDB is on 3306 — that's why the compose maps 6967/6969 instead. the notes' habit applies: know what's listening before binding ( netstat prints nothing when the port is free): bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr 6967 netstat -ano | findstr 6969 if the personal manual-run containers from Docker ( EB_mysql , EB_phpmyadmin ) are still around, remove them first — they're registered on the same host ports and names can clash: bash Copy docker rm -f EB_mysql EB_phpmyadmin 1d — up + verify + lifecycle DISCLAIMER the following commands WILL NOT WORK if the terminal you are using is NOT inside the root folder of your project. bash Copy docker compose up -d docker compose ps # expect eb-mysql & eb-phpmyadmin, both "Up" docker exec -it eb-mysql mysql --version # expect 8.0.x optional — inspect the network the compose file created (both containers should appear as endpoints on it): bash Copy docker network inspect eb-network phpMyAdmin answers at http://localhost:6969 — log in with the MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD from .env (or the ebuser account for day-to-day work). the compose lifecycle from the notes: bash Copy docker compose stop # stops both, containers stay registered docker compose down -v # stops AND wipes containers + eb-db-data (blank start again) down -v deletes whatever data you typed into phpMyAdmin use stop for day-to-day shutdowns. down -v = reset-to-blank; only when you want the DB re-seeded. -v = vanishes — it never saves; it erases. 1e — wipe-day recovery loop (for when down -v is the class norm) if the workflow wipes regularly, recovering is a standard loop, not a panic: migrate rebuilds the structure, the seed file rebuilds the contents. event what's in the volume what I do first-ever up -d empty eb_shop , zero tables doctrine:migrations:migrate — once stop / down (no -v ) / reboot / closing apps volume survives — schema and rows intact nothing down -v → up -d blank again (Docker auto-creates empty eb_shop from .env ) migrate (structure) + seed import (rows) running migrate when already migrated the doctrine_migration_versions table inside the DB stamps what's done prints Nothing to migrate — always safe to re-run mental model entities = blueprint code — they never "run". the migration is the to-do list SQL generated from them, executed only on a blank database; the stamp lives inside the database itself, which is why the same file rebuilds it identically every wipe. powershell Copy # 1. structure — always first, always safe to re-run symfony console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction # 2. contents — after the migration, pour the seed file back in Get-Content .\eb_shop_seed.sql -Raw | docker compose exec -T eb-mysql mysql -u root -pebRootPass1 --default-character-set=utf8mb4 eb_shop (GUI alternative: phpMyAdmin → Import tab — same result.) the seed file is made once , whenever the data looks good, and re-made whenever you've typed more: powershell Copy docker exec eb-mysql mysqldump -u root -pebRootPass1 --default-character-set=utf8mb4 eb_shop > eb_shop_seed.sql (phpMyAdmin route: eb_shop → Export → Save — identical outcome.) the seed file holds password hashes + emails keep it OUT of the git repo. store it beside the vault notes, or in the project root after eb_shop_seed.sql is in .gitignore . Step 2 — .env the professor-format compose pulls four values straight from this file ( MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD , MYSQL_DATABASE , MYSQL_USER , MYSQL_PASSWORD ), and the DATABASE_URL at the bottom already interpolates MYSQL_* for Symfony itself — so this one file feeds both worlds: key XAMPP value new value MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD — new key — e.g. eb_root_cap — the container's root password, used for in-container admin + phpMyAdmin root login MYSQL_USER root ebuser — a dedicated app user, NOT root MYSQL_PASSWORD (empty) the ebuser password — this is what Symfony connects with MYSQL_IP 127.0.0.1 keep MYSQL_PORT 3306 6967 (compose maps it) MYSQL_DATABASE eb_shop keep root vs app user root ( MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD ) is for inside-the-container admin work and phpMyAdmin root logins. the app itself talks through ebuser — same split the notes bake into their compose block. and bump the server version in the DATABASE_URL line — MariaDB → MySQL: env Copy DATABASE_URL="mysql://${MYSQL_USER}:${MYSQL_PASSWORD}@${MYSQL_IP}:${MYSQL_PORT}/${MYSQL_DATABASE}?serverVersion=8.0.36&charset=utf8mb4" password with special characters DATABASE_URL is still a URL — characters like @ : / ? # inside the password must be percent-encoded (e.g. @ → %40 ). plain alphanumeric passwords avoid the whole issue. sanity checks before making entities: bash Copy symfony console dbal:run-sql "SELECT 1" # optional, but catches a wrong .env before make:entity does docker exec -it eb-mysql mysql -u root -p -e "SHOW DATABASES;" # eb_shop should exist Step 3 — entities via make:entity how to read these tables run the command, then follow the rows top to bottom. Enter = just press enter to accept the bracketed default. make:entity auto-creates the id field on every new entity — and it lands as a plain id column , not *_id (learned the hard way: the first migrate died because FKs pointed at users.id , which doesn't exist). after the run the AI pinned every PK with #[ORM\Column(name: ...)] → product_id , order_id , item_id , image_id — one-line edits, nothing to type in the terminal. naming strategy in config/packages/doctrine.yaml is underscore , so camelCase properties auto-map to snake_case columns ( userName → user_name ). no need to type column names anywhere. wording of prompts can differ slightly between maker versions — match by meaning . watch the "new field name inside entity" prompt — it arrives right after answering "add a property on <Other> yes". that's naming the collection on the OTHER class ( $user->getOrders() ), not a field of yours. the bracketed default ( orders , orderItems ) is the one the doc expects → press Enter . User — already exists, skip it src/Entity/User.php is already set up (security-bundle style) and mapped to users : property column notes id user_id id username user_name length 255 (bumped from 100 to match XAMPP) email user_email length 180 , unique index (XAMPP had none) role user_role length 50, PHP default 'customer' password user_password length 255 profilePic user_profile_pic nullable since the target DB is blank and built from entities, the entity's lengths win — and they ended up matching XAMPP: user_name was bumped to 255, while the 180-char unique email and varchar(50) role stay as two intentionally-accepted, data-safe differences (all 11 old emails are distinct; role values all fit in 50). Product bash Copy symfony console make:entity Product property name → Enter field type follow-up prompts creates productName Enter (=string) length Enter (255) → nullable Enter (no) product_name varchar(255) productDescription text nullable Enter (no) product_description text productPrice decimal precision Enter (10) → scale Enter (2) → nullable Enter (no) product_price decimal(10,2) productStockQuantity integer nullable Enter (no) product_stock_quantity int productImg Enter (=string) length Enter (255) → nullable Enter (no) product_img varchar(255) Enter (empty) — stops adding fields done Order bash Copy symfony console make:entity Order property name → Enter field type follow-up prompts creates user relation related class User → type 0 (many to one) → nullable no → add property on User yes → field name inside User: Enter (accept default orders — do NOT type a field name here) → orphanRemoval no user_id , FK → users.user_id totalAmount decimal precision Enter (10) → scale Enter (2) → nullable Enter (no) total_amount decimal(10,2) orderDate datetime nullable Enter (no) order_date datetime status Enter (=string) length 50 → nullable Enter (no) status varchar(50) Enter (empty) — stops done then pin the identifiers (AI-applied after make:entity — all five entities got the full treatment in the end): php Copy #[ORM \Entity ( repositoryClass : OrderRepository :: class ) ] #[ORM \Table ( name : 'orders' ) ] // ← table pin (already in this step) // on the id field: #[ORM\Column(name: 'order_id')] // PK pin // on the user relation: #[ORM\JoinColumn(name: 'user_id', referencedColumnName: 'user_id', ...)] // FK pin why that line matters order is a reserved word in MySQL. the XAMPP table is named orders (plural), and Doctrine's underscore naming would default the new entity to table order . this single line pins the table name so the migration generates orders cleanly. OrderItem bash Copy symfony console make:entity OrderItem property name → Enter field type follow-up prompts creates maker blocks reserved words as FIELD names too order cannot be typed as a property name — [ERROR] Name "order" is a reserved word. (it would produce an order column). the shop's workaround: name the relation field orderRef , and the AI pins the column back to order_id with a JoinColumn line. bottom line for you: different word in the terminal, same database table. property name → Enter field type follow-up prompts creates orderRef relation related class Order → ManyToOne → nullable no (typed — default is yes ) → add property on Order Enter (yes) → field name inside Order: Enter (accept whatever it offers — AI renames it to orderItems after) → orphanRemoval Enter (no) column gets pinned to order_id , FK → orders.order_id product relation related class Product → ManyToOne → nullable no (typed!) → add property on Product no (typed — no inverse wanted) product_id , FK → products.product_id quantity integer nullable Enter (no) quantity int priceAtPurchase decimal precision Enter (10) → scale Enter (2) → nullable Enter (no) price_at_purchase decimal(10,2) Enter (empty) — stops done side note: the inverse (the yes on "add property on Order") gives the Order class a collection of its line items — the AI later renames it orderItems — which restores the old app's ability to read an order's line items. Image bash Copy symfony console make:entity Image property name → Enter field type follow-up prompts creates filename Enter (=string) length Enter (255) → nullable Enter (no) filename varchar(255) originalName Enter (=string) length Enter (255) → nullable Enter (no) original_name varchar(255) uploadedBy relation related class User → 0 (many to one) → nullable yes → add property on User no uploaded_by , FK → users.user_id , nullable uploadedAt datetime nullable Enter (no) uploaded_at datetime Enter (empty) — stops done two small differences vs XAMPP XAMPP had a unique key on filename . to keep it, add unique: true to the column attribute (one-line code change — the AI can do it after entities are made). XAMPP had uploaded_at ... DEFAULT current_timestamp() . plain Doctrine has no column default, so each new row must set it in code — a constructor like $this->uploadedAt = new \DateTimeImmutable(); does it. AI-job again; just flag it during coding. Step 4 — migrations (blank DB, so this runs for real) bash Copy symfony console make:migration open the generated file in /migrations/ and skim it. expected content: CREATE TABLE for product , orders , order_item , image (+ users if the users table isn't there yet) foreign keys on orders.user_id , order_item.order_id , order_item.product_id , image.uploaded_by unique index on users.user_email all columns snake_case — if any come out camelCase, something ate the naming strategy; stop and check doctrine.yaml review before running on this fresh database the migration should only contain CREATE/ADD statements. any DROP / RENAME is a red flag — read it before running. bash Copy symfony console doctrine:migrations:migrate confirm with yes , then validate: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:schema:validate expected tail: [OK] The ORM mapping of the entity classes is valid. and [OK] The mapping on the database is in sync with the current mapping metadata. — on a blank DB freshly migrated, both should pass clean. do NOT import the XAMPP dump before migrating the flow is entities → migration → migrate on an empty schema. importing SQL first (the old-phpMyAdmin reflex) makes make:migration produce conflicting drop/alter diffs against what came in. entities first, migrate second, data last. Reference — the source schema (from XAMPP) numbers as of Nov 2026: users 11 , products 5 , orders 5 , order_items 10 , images 7 . all InnoDB , utf8mb4 / utf8mb4_general_ci . users column type flags user_id int PK, AI user_name varchar(255) not null user_email varchar(255) not null user_password varchar(255) not null — 60-char bcrypt ( password_hash ) user_role varchar(255) default 'customer' — values seen: customer , admin , banned user_profile_pic varchar(255) nullable products column type flags product_id int PK, AI product_name varchar(255) not null product_description text not null product_price decimal(10,2) not null product_stock_quantity int not null product_img varchar(255) not null — filename from the images table orders column type flags order_id int PK, AI user_id int FK → users.user_id , not null total_amount decimal(10,2) not null order_date datetime not null status varchar(50) not null — all rows currently pending order_items column type flags item_id int PK, AI order_id int FK → orders.order_id , not null product_id int FK → products.product_id , not null quantity int not null price_at_purchase decimal(10,2) not null images column type flags image_id int PK, AI filename varchar(255) not null, unique original_name varchar(255) not null uploaded_by int FK → users.user_id , nullable, ON DELETE SET NULL uploaded_at timestamp default current_timestamp() data quirks worth remembering ids have gaps ( order_id 3 , image_id 4 missing, AUTO_INCREMENTs beyond max) — those are just deleted rows, not corruption. user 16 ( enric ) has role banned — the existing User::getRoles() only maps admin , so banned-user handling is still unsolved on the PHP side; note it for the AI during coding. totals check out mathematically: order 1 = 6×110 + 2×140 + 4×150 + 3×200 + 54 = 2,194.00 ✓, order 6 = 35×150 = 5,250.00 ✓. stock decrements left a trace: product 5 was bought 35× and its stock is now 3 . h: 1. Don't Forget the Viewport Tag First
pages.b: CSS3 @media Queries Guide Media queries ( @media ) in CSS3 allow you to apply specific styles based on a device's characteristics—such as screen width, height, orientation, or user preferences like dark mode. They are the foundation of responsive web design , ensuring your site looks great on smartphones, tablets, and desktop displays alike. 1. Don't Forget the Viewport Tag First Before @media queries will work properly on mobile devices, you must include this <meta> tag inside your HTML <head> section: html Copy < meta name = "viewport" content = "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" > Note Without this, mobile browsers will pretend they are desktop browsers and zoom out, breaking your responsive layouts. 2. Basic Syntax A media query consists of a media type , optional logical operators , and media features inside parentheses: css Copy @media media-type and (media-feature) { /* CSS rules go here */ } Media Types: screen (computer/phone screens), print (print preview/paper), all (default for all devices). Media Features: min-width , max-width , orientation , prefers-color-scheme , etc. 3. How to Structure Media Queries Approach A: Mobile-First (Recommended) Write base styles for mobile screens first, then use min-width queries to add or adjust styles as the screen gets wider. css Copy /* Base styles (Mobile) */ .container { width : 100% ; padding : 10px ; } /* Tablet and larger (768px and up) */ @media screen and ( min-width : 768px ) { .container { width : 80% ; padding : 20px ; } } /* Desktop and larger (1024px and up) */ @media screen and ( min-width : 1024px ) { .container { width : 1200px ; margin : 0 auto; } } Approach B: Desktop-First Write base styles for large screens first, then use max-width queries to adjust styles as the viewport shrinks. css Copy /* Base styles (Desktop) */ .sidebar { width : 300px ; float : left; } /* Mobile (767px or smaller) */ @media screen and ( max-width : 767px ) { .sidebar { width : 100% ; float : none; } } 4. Common Breakpoint Quick Reference While exact breakpoints depend on your design, these industry standards are a great starting point: Device Category Recommended Breakpoint Example Query Small Phones < 480px Default (Mobile-first base styles) Mobiles / Small Tablets 481px – 768px @media (min-width: 481px) Tablets / Small Laptops 769px – 1024px @media (min-width: 769px) Desktops 1025px – 1200px @media (min-width: 1025px) Large Screens / TV > 1200px @media (min-width: 1201px) 5. Useful Advanced Examples Combining Conditions ( and , , ) Use and to combine rules: css Copy /* Applies only if screen is between 600px and 900px */ @media screen and ( min-width : 600px ) and ( max-width : 900px ) { body { background-color : lightblue; } } Use a comma , to act as an OR operator: css Copy /* Applies if screen is in landscape OR width is at least 1200px */ @media ( orientation : landscape), ( min-width : 1200px ) { .hero { height : 100vh ; } } Modern Feature Queries Dark Mode Preference: css Copy @media ( prefers-color-scheme : dark) { body { background-color : #121212 ; color : #ffffff ; } } Print Styles: css Copy @media print { .no-print { display : none; } body { color : #000 ; } } See also CSS3 and CSS Frameworks — the master css note this sits inside Measurement Units — px, em, rem — what the breakpoints are made of CSS Variables — keeping palettes consistent across breakpoints

pages.b: DISCLAIMER Everything in here is assuming you put your project in the root folder of your server. What if i put my project in a subfolder? assuming your subfolder is named project just add project/ to everything mentioning localhost/ or yourwebsite.com/ it should look like this localhost/project/ and/or yourwebsite.com/project/ Source Config Files this file is named config.php and sits inside the root folder of your website What does it do? It basically gives your entire workspace something to reference to so that doing back links like ../../ is not required. The Code ( config.php ) copy this if you like php Copy <?php // defining variables $dir = str_replace ( '\\' , '/' , __DIR__ ); $docRoot = str_replace ( '\\' , '/' , $_SERVER [ 'DOCUMENT_ROOT' ]); $web_path = str_replace ( $docRoot , '' , $dir ); define ( 'BASE_URL' , $web_path . '/' ); //project directory define ( 'ROOT_DIR' , __DIR__ . '/' ); //php server directory ?> this is the most basic config file i could think of this is dynamic so if you put the project in subfolders, it would still work! What's the difference between BASE_URL and ROOT_DIR the main difference between the two is how they reference files BASE_URL translates to yourwebsite.com/ or localhost/ you use it to reference pages ROOT_DIR translates to your/path/to/php/server/ or in LAMP it's var/www/html/ you use it to reference files (like the components/header.php example below) How to use? html Copy < header > < h1 > ESTRERA BOTANICALS </ h1 > < nav > <!-- if your website has an index.php on root you can use BASE_URL --> <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/" or "localhost/"--> < a href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>" > HOME </ a > <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/about-us" or localhost/about-us--> < a href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>about-us" > ABOUT US </ a > <!-- or if you prefer your files to be all in the root. you can do this --> <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/shop.php" or "localhost/"--> < a class = "heading-nav" href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>shop.php" > SHOP </ a > </ nav > </ header > referencing webpages using BASE_URL html Copy < link rel = "stylesheet" href = "<?=BASE_URL?>style.css" > php Copy <?php require ROOT_DIR . 'components/header.php' ?> referencing files using ROOT_DIR . also discussed further in OOP on html and look at its implementation OOP on html one nice thing about php is that you can spawn an instance of an object inside your website. this is very useful when dealing with html that is used on multiple pages and just copy pasting it. let's call those objects as Components Prerequisite under is assuming you learned about Source Config Files , if you haven't please look at it first before reading any further how it looks like instead of copy and pasting a header in another website. you can simply put the entire component inside a php file. for example: header.php html Copy < header > < h1 > ESTRERA BOTANICALS </ h1 > < nav > < a class = "heading-nav" href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>" > HOME </ a > < a class = "heading-nav" href = "#none" > SHOP </ a > < a class = "heading-nav" href = "#none" > BEST SELLERS </ a > < a class = "heading-nav" href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>/about-us" > ABOUT US </ a > < a class = "heading-nav" id = "heading-cta-button" href = "#none" > Shop Now </ a > </ nav > </ header > i want to put this on all my webpages how to implement it php Copy <?php //do not forget config.php require_once '../config.php' ; ?> <html lang= "en" > <head> <meta charset= "UTF-8" > <meta name= "viewport" content= "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" > <title>About Us</title> <link rel= "stylesheet" href= "../style.css" > </head> <body> <!-- an "AHA!" moment here. always loved oop --> <?php require ROOT_DIR . 'components/header.php' ?> </body> </html> since the header is inside the body we reference the component using <?php require ROOT_DIR . 'components/header.php' ?>

a pseudo class is a keyword added to a selector that styles an element based on its specific state or condition , rather than its static position in the document tree. the classic one — a button that reacts when you hover it: css Copy /* base button layout */ button { background-color : darkblue; color : white; transition : background-color 0.3s ease; } /* color swap while hovered */ button :hover { background-color : royalblue; } /* shrink button effect while pressed down */ button :active { transform : scale ( 0.95 ); } the usual suspects pseudo class styles the element while... :hover the pointer is over it :active it is being pressed down :focus it is selected (clicked or tabbed to) :first-child it is the first child of its parent :last-child it is the last child of its parent :checked a checkbox / radio is on :visited a link has already been visited See also types of selectors — the thing pseudo classes attach themselves to CSS transitions — makes the hover change smooth instead of an instant snap CSS transforms — what scale(0.95) up there is from
