Docker What is Docker? docker is an app that makes migrating systems, servers, databases, etc. a lot easier. the way docker does it is with images and containers . just let the next machine install docker only , and it's ready to migrate! What if we don't use docker? if you don't use docker when migrating, the system might break. it could be because of: outdated / unstable software, no prerequisite packages, inconsistent configuration, and more. Images images are one of the key features of docker. images are packages that are ready to be copied and deployed to your container so it can be used immediately. Analogy think of an image as a photo of a document. you can still read the document right? but you can't edit it, just scan it. once the image has been scanned, it can then be edited again and be used again. in plainer terms: the image is the frozen package — you don't touch it yourself. you run it, and what's running it is the container. one image can spawn as many copies of a container as you want. Containers containers are also one of the key features of docker. containers are basically tiny virtual machines with their own apps and services running — and those services would be your running images. Setting up docker Images needed mysql php Create network bash Copy docker network create [name of network] Example bash Copy docker network create webdev-network most basic command to create a container DISCLAIMER NOT RECOMMENDED TO RUN THIS BY ITSELF bash Copy docker run -d [name of container] why it's not recommended a bare run like this has no network, no volume, no environment variables, nothing. the full versions below include all of those — use those instead. command to find if a port is used (windows) bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr [portnumber] Example bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr 3306 if something is using port 3306 , you get output like this. if the port is free, the command just prints nothing. Copy TCP 0.0.0.0:3306 0.0.0.0:0 LISTENING 18196 TCP [::]:3306 [::]:0 LISTENING 18196 Creating containers MySQL container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -v [Volume Name]:[Volume Location] -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=[Mysql Password] -e MYSQL_DATABASE=[DatabaseName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-mysql --network webdev-network -v webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=webdev-db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 phpMyAdmin container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -e PMA_HOST=[MysqlContainerName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-phpmyadmin --network webdev-network -e PMA_HOST=webdev-mysql -p 3311:80 phpmyadmin My command DISCLAIMER DO NOT COPY THIS. THIS COMMAND IS IRRELEVANT TO YOUR PROJECTS bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_mysql --network EB_Network -v EB-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=EB_shop -p 6967:3306 mysql:8.0 bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_phpmyadmin --network EB_Network -e PMA_HOST=EB_mysql -p 6969:80 phpmyadmin Extra docker commands from the notes of Sir Ariel Bensing. Build an image from a dockerfile bash Copy docker build -t symfony-app . the . at the end matters — it points to the dockerfile in the current folder . Build the container based on the image bash Copy docker run --name symfony-app-demo --network platform-network -p 8000:8000 symfony-app Create a network bash Copy docker network create platform-network Build a container for MySQL bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-db --network platform-network -v symfony-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=app_db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 Build a container for phpMyAdmin bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-pma --network platform-network -p 8081:80 -e PMA_HOST=symfony-db phpmyadmin Execute a command inside a running container bash Copy docker exec -it symfony-app-demo "symfony command" Inspect a network bash Copy docker network inspect [network name] Delete a network bash Copy docker network rm [network name] Delete a container bash Copy docker rm [container name] Delete an image bash Copy docker rmi [image name] Stop a container bash Copy docker stop [container name] took me a while to realize stop is for containers, not networks lmao. networks don't stop, they just exist until you rm them. Connecting Symfony to the database on symfony to connect to your database you have to open your .env file on the root folder. Making variables env Copy MYSQL_USER= MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP= MYSQL_PORT= MYSQL_DATABASE= Example my database has these variables to connect to. it doesn't mean you can copy this and make it work on yours — you have to provide your own values. env Copy MYSQL_USER=root MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP=127.0.0.1 MYSQL_PORT=3306 MYSQL_DATABASE=eb_shop Connecting to database using the variables from #Making variables to connect to the database: env Copy DATABASE_URL="mysql://${MYSQL_USER}:${MYSQL_PASSWORD}@${MYSQL_IP}:${MYSQL_PORT}/${MYSQL_DATABASE}?serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB&charset=utf8mb4" you can copy this one if you want. drop database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:drop --force create database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:create Using compose.yaml spelling the file is named compose.yaml — compose , not composer . composer is the PHP package thing, easy to mix up. both files exist in a symfony project and they do totally different jobs. using compose.yaml is one of the great things of Symfony and docker. it allows you to create containers when needed and delete them when not used or powered off. it also allows you to migrate your project easily, because the whole setup is stored in the project itself and not inside a separate database. it's all in one file. IMPORTANT change your compose.override.yaml to compose.override-disabled.yaml or basically delete it so that it doesn't interfere with your development. Editing compose.yaml everything inside this file is the same thing the manual docker run commands did earlier. what this basically does is create 2 containers named webdev-mysql and webdev-phpmyadmin , and their images are in the name. yaml Copy services: webdev-mysql: image: mysql:8.0 container_name: webdev-mysql restart: unless-stopped environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD} MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE} MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER} MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD} ports: - "6666:3306" volumes: - webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql networks: - webdev-network webdev-phpmyadmin: image: phpmyadmin container_name: webdev-phpmyadmin restart: unless-stopped environment: PMA_HOST: webdev-mysql ports: - "7777:80" networks: - webdev-network volumes: webdev-db-data: networks: webdev-network: this file is also connected to the .env file — that's why you see those ${MYSQL_DATABASE} things. selectors are how you tell css which element(s) to style. same declarations, different targets. ID selector use the id selector whenever you only need one element to be edited by css. prefix: # html Copy <!-- correct — one element, one id --> < h2 id = "about_me" > </ h2 > <!-- wrong — dili pwede kaduha, ID is unique. (an id must appear only once per page) --> < h3 id = "about_me" > </ h3 > Class selector use the class selector when you want multiple elements to update when one class is edited. prefix: . html Copy < h4 class = "this_class" > </ h4 > < h2 class = "this_class" > </ h2 > < body class = "two_times" > </ body > the same class can sit on as many tags as you want — that's the point of it. css Copy #about_me {} /* singular — only grabs the one id */ .this_class { /* grabs every tag wearing this class */ font-size : 40px ; } .two_times { scale : 2em ; } Element selector uses the tag name and automatically sets every instance of it on the page: css Copy h2 { /* every <h2>, no id or class needed */ } Attribute selector grabs elements that carry a specific attribute: css Copy input [type] { /* any <input> that has a type attribute at all */ } Grouping selector stack any other kind of selector together with commas — they all receive the same declarations: css Copy .this , h1 , h2 {} Universal selector targets everything on the page: css Copy * {}

routers ( WRT300N ) prepare the end devices (server, pcs, smartphone) the cabling rule used all through this build gigabit ports are reserved for switch↔switch and switch↔router links first, fast ethernet is for end devices (pcs, servers, the wrt300n lan side, phones) connect the pcs and server to their switches connect them all using straight through cables on fast ethernet ports configuration switch0 Fa0/1 to server0 Fa0 switch0 Fa0/2 to pc0 Fa0 switch0 Fa0/3 to wireless router0 switch1 Fa0/1 to pc4 Fa0 switch1 Fa0/2 to pc5 Fa0 switch1 Fa0/3 to wireless router1 switch2 Fa0/1 to pc2 Fa0 switch2 Fa0/2 to pc3 Fa0 switch4 Fa0/1 to pc7 Fa0 switch4 Fa0/2 to pc8 Fa0 switch4 Fa0/3 to pc9 Fa0 connect the switches to each other every switch↔switch link is a cross over cable on gigabit ports — these all become trunks later configuration multilayer switch0 Gig0/1 to switch1 Gig0/1 multilayer switch0 Gig0/2 to switch0 Gig0/1 switch0 Gig0/2 to switch3 Gig0/1 switch3 Gig0/2 to switch4 Gig0/1 connect the 1941 router straight through cables — the router side is always one of its two gigabit ports, the switch side is the free gig port configuration router0 Gig0/0 or Gig0/1 to switch1 (hover the cable ends to check which is which — it doesn't matter, no ips go on the router) router0 other gig port to switch2 Gig0/1 add the wireless routers wireless router0 → switch0 and wireless router1 → switch1, straight through into the wrt300n's internet port. then pc1/pc6 into its lan ports and smartphone0 connects over wifi Full tree the setup before anything, remember the exit ritual you'll do over and over: no shutdown → exit → do wr — exit guide who owns what the 3560 owns every gateway ( 192.168.x.1 ) — same rule as the dhcp lab, no other device gets an svi with an ip. ping each other while the router doesn't route dhcp pool (back on the main switch) this is what makes vlan 10 special — everything below happens on the 3560's cli (config mode). click back to the main device first exclude the gateway address first a pool leases the whole /24 starting at .1 unless told not to — and .1 is the svi you just made prompt: Switch(config)# cisco Copy Switch(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 Switch(config)# do wr create the vlan10 pool prompt: Switch(config)# cisco Copy ip dhcp pool vlan10 the prompt changes to Switch(dhcp-config)# — a pool needs 3 things: cisco Copy Switch(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 Switch(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.10.1 Switch(dhcp-config)# dns-server 192.168.10.1 Switch(dhcp-config)# exit Switch(config)# do wr what the 3 lines mean network — the range being handed out: 192.168.10.0/24 (minus the excluded .1 ) default-router — the gateway pushed to the pc = the vlan 10 svi dns-server — here it matches the svi too this is the only pool — vlans 20/30/100/200 are all static. and don't add svis on the sub switches, the 3560 stays the only ip owner enable ip routing same "optional but do it" step as the other labs — without it the pcs can never ping across vlans — ip routing guide cisco Copy Switch(config)# ip routing Switch(config)# do wr switched the pool on late and a pc already grabbed a bad lease? clear the lease table and let the pcs re-request — toggle the pc static→dhcp too if it's stubborn cisco Copy Switch# clear ip dhcp binding * the router (1941) turn the ports on — and that's it click the router → cli tab — enable guide (same ritual, the prompt says Router instead of Switch ) cisco Copy Router> enable Router# configure terminal Router(config)# cisco Copy pc3 works (same vlan, same switch — plain layer 2) pc2/pc3 → anything outside switch2 fails — their pod is stranded behind the router. expected, don't chase it wireless routers (WRT300N) these are configured in their gui , not the cli. each one gets its internet port parked inside vlan 20 so the routers themselves can reach the network internet port — static ip click wrt300n0 → gui/setup → SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) Definition An SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) is a virtual layer 3 interface that belongs to an entire VLAN instead of a physical port. It is software-only — there is no physical jack for it — and it exists inside the switch itself. what it does it is the one interface created per VLAN : interface vlan [number] creates the SVI for that VLAN its IP address is the gateway for that whole VLAN — every pc in the vlan points its default gateway at the SVI's IP it is also how you give the switch itself a management IP so you can reach it over the network on a multilayer switch like the 3560, inter-vlan traffic is routed between SVIs — that's why ip routing must be on, since the 3560 does not route between SVIs by default how you configure it from the notes — enter the SVI, give it an IP, then the exit ritual: cisco Copy Switch(config)# interface vlan 200 Switch(config-if)# ip address 192.168.5.1 255.255.255.0 Switch(config-if)# no shutdown Switch(config-if)# exit Switch(config)# do wr Switch(config-if)# is the prompt while inside the SVI when the SVI comes up you see %LINK-5-CHANGED: Interface Vlan200, changed state to up SVIs from the labs lab SVI ip address gateway for basic setup Vlan200 FACULTY 192.168.5.1 pc0 (192.168.5.10) basic setup Vlan300 STUDENT 192.168.10.1 pc1 (192.168.10.10) intermediate setup Vlan100 STAFF 192.168.100.1 pc0 + pc3 intermediate setup Vlan200 PRESS 192.168.200.1 pc1 + server0 intermediate setup Vlan300 ACCOUNTING 192.168.50.1 pc2 SVI vs physical interface SVI physical interface (e.g. Fa0/1, Gi0/1) exists per VLAN actual port tied to hardware no — virtual yes typical use vlan gateway / management / routing access port, trunk port common exam trap creating the VLAN ( vlan 200 ) is not the same as creating its SVI ( interface vlan 200 ). the VLAN is the layer 2 broadcast domain; the SVI is the layer 3 interface on top of it. a VLAN with no SVI has no gateway. verify cisco Copy show ip interface brief shows the SVIs as Vlan200 , Vlan300 , etc. with their IPs — in the labs they should show up/up after no shutdown . sources: Cisco Basic Setup · Cisco Intermediate Setup · Cisco Commands

Notes Cisco Intermediate Setup Cisco Basic Setup the full packet tracer lab walkthrough. starts with the scenario, then how to build the topology (3560 + 2950, crossover between switches, straight-through to the pcs), then every command needed to finish it end to end — vlan 200 then vlan 300 (create + name + svi) on the main switch, trunks on both switches, the same vlans created on the 2950, access ports for pc0/pc1, both pc's ip/gateway setup, optional ip routing so the pcs can talk across vlans, and how to verify/ping. DHCP Basic Setup the dhcp version of the two-vlan lab. same 3560 + 2960 topology and same STUDENT/FACULTY svis, but the main switch serves the ip addresses itself: ip dhcp excluded-address for the gateways, pools vlan100 / vlan200 with network + default-router + dns-server , ip routing , and the pcs set to dhcp in packet tracer. carries the debugging lesson from this run — no interface vlan svis on the sub switch, because a duplicate 192.168.x.1 triggers %DHCPD-4-PING_CONFLICT and kills pings (fix: no interface vlan 100/200 , clear ip dhcp binding * , renew on the pcs). Cisco Commands the raw cisco command reference the setup pulls from. every command shows the prompt you should see before typing it ( Switch> , Switch(config)# , Switch(config-if)# ...), with working examples (vlan 200/faculty), per-device warnings (the 3560 needs switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q , the 2950 doesn't support it), the no shutdown / exit / do wr exit ritual, and the trunk/vlan/verify commands. routers

pages.b: skr canvas 🚀 Help me to become a full-time open-source developer by sponsoring me on Github Google Skia binding to Node.js via Node-API , 0 System dependencies! 中文文档 Install bash Copy yarn add @napi-rs/canvas npm install @napi-rs/canvas Support matrix System requirement arm64 cortex-a57 or newer CPU architecture on Linux . All Apple M chips on macOS . armv7 cortex-a7 or newer CPU architecture. glibc Since Skia relies on the glibc 2.18 API, you need to have at least glibc version >= 2.18 on your system. AWS Lambda usage To use this library on Lambda you will need to use a Lambda layer. You can simply attach a lambda layer by getting an ARN from Canvas-Lambda-Layer Make sure to exclude @napi-rs/canvas while bundling your Lambda. Usage js Copy const { promises } = require ( 'node:fs' ) const { join } = require ( 'node:path' ) const { createCanvas, loadImage } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) const canvas = createCanvas ( 300 , 320 ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) ctx. lineWidth = 10 ctx. strokeStyle = '#03a9f4' ctx. fillStyle = '#03a9f4' // Wall ctx. strokeRect ( 75 , 140 , 150 , 110 ) // Door ctx. fillRect ( 130 , 190 , 40 , 60 ) // Roof ctx. beginPath () ctx. moveTo ( 50 , 140 ) ctx. lineTo ( 150 , 60 ) ctx. lineTo ( 250 , 140 ) ctx. closePath () ctx. stroke () async function main ( ) { // load images from disk or from a URL const catImage = await loadImage ( 'path/to/cat.png' ) const dogImage = await loadImage ( 'https://example.com/path/to/dog.jpg' ) ctx. drawImage (catImage, 0 , 0 , catImage. width , catImage. height ) ctx. drawImage (dogImage, canvas. width / 2 , canvas. height / 2 , dogImage. width , dogImage. height ) // export canvas as image const pngData = await canvas. encode ( 'png' ) // JPEG, AVIF and WebP are also supported // encoding in libuv thread pool, non-blocking await promises. writeFile ( join (__dirname, 'simple.png' ), pngData) } main () Image metadata toBuffer , encode and encodeSync can write the resolution (DPI) and a few text fields into PNG and JPEG output. Put them in the options object: js Copy const png = canvas. toBuffer ( 'image/png' , { resolution : 300 , // pixels per inch, the same option as node-canvas title : 'Floor plan' , author : 'Jane Doe' , description : 'Ground floor, 1:100' , }) // JPEG: use encode / encodeSync to set the quality as well const jpeg = await canvas. encode ( 'jpeg' , { quality : 90 , resolution : 300 , copyright : '© 2026 Jane Doe' }) Option PNG JPEG resolution pHYs chunk JFIF density (dots per inch) title Title text chunk XMP dc:title author Author XMP dc:creator description Description XMP dc:description copyright Copyright XMP dc:rights software Software XMP xmp:CreatorTool comment Comment COM segment WebP, AVIF and GIF output ignore these options. toDataURL , toDataURLAsync , toBlob , convertToBlob , encodeStream and savePng never write metadata. To save a file with metadata, write the Buffer from toBuffer or encode . With an options object, toBuffer('image/jpeg', ...) encodes at quality 92; use encode or encodeSync for another quality. Text rendering By default text looks the same on every OS. Every font is drawn with FreeType, with Skia's default text gamma, no LCD (subpixel) text and one font family table (the one Linux uses). The same font files give the same pixels and the same measureText results on macOS, Linux and Windows. To get the same output everywhere, register your own font files under names no OS installs, and draw only with those names: js Copy const { GlobalFonts } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) GlobalFonts . registerFromPath ( './fonts/Lato-Regular.ttf' , 'MyLato' ) ctx. font = '20px MyLato' These still depend on the OS and the machine: Installed fonts. Names like Arial or Helvetica , and the generic families ( sans-serif , serif , monospace , system-ui , the canvas default 10px sans-serif ) resolve to whatever is installed. Characters your registered fonts lack. They are taken from the installed default fonts when those have them, else they draw as boxes. There is no search through all installed fonts. The ex , ch , cap and line-height units inside SVG images use an installed default font. Lottie (Skottie) text uses installed fonts. PDF font embedding depends on the build target. x64 and arm64 builds can differ by 1 color level on some edge pixels. A FREETYPE_PROPERTIES env var changes FreeType's hinting. Set DISABLE_SYSTEM_FONTS_LOAD=1 to keep installed fonts out of GlobalFonts.families . By default they can still be found by name, on every OS. setTextRenderer() setTextRenderer('system') draws text the way Chrome does on each OS: CoreText on macOS (with CoreText's installed fonts and fallback), Fontations on Linux and FreeType on Windows, plus each OS's text gamma, LCD text on opaque macOS canvases, Chrome's per-OS font families and the macOS metric rules. This was the default in 1.0.12 and 1.0.13. 'portable' is the default. js Copy const { setTextRenderer, getTextRenderer } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) setTextRenderer ( 'system' ) getTextRenderer () // 'system' It applies to the whole process. Call it once at startup, before you create canvases. setTextRenderer('portable') switches back. Any other value throws a TypeError . A canvas created before the switch keeps its old text gamma until you set its width or height. A ctx.font value set before the switch keeps its parsed form (sizes in ex , ch and other font-relative units, and on macOS the BlinkMacSystemFont to system-ui rewrite), so set ctx.font again after the switch. Behavior change ( #1402 ): text on macOS and Linux is drawn the way Windows draws it, so pixels and measureText results differ from 1.0.12 and 1.0.13. On macOS, the installed fonts are FreeType faces again (as in 1.0.11), read from /System/Library/Fonts , /Library/Fonts and ~/Library/Fonts ; CoreText's per-character fallback is off, and sans-serif , serif and monospace map to Arial, Times New Roman and the Linux monospace list. On macOS, DISABLE_SYSTEM_FONTS_LOAD no longer hides installed fonts from name lookup, as on Linux and Windows and before 1.0.12; it only keeps them out of GlobalFonts.families . Call setTextRenderer('system') to get the 1.0.12 / 1.0.13 behavior back. Load Animation js Copy const { LottieAnimation } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) // Load from file const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) // Load from JSON string with resource path for external assets const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromData (jsonString, { resourcePath : '/path/to/assets' , }) Animation Properties js Copy animation. duration // Total duration in seconds animation. fps // Frames per second animation. frames // Total frame count animation. width // Animation width animation. height // Animation height animation. version // Lottie format version Playback Control js Copy animation. seekFrame ( 30 ) // Seek to frame 30 animation. seek ( 1.5 ) // Seek to 1.5 seconds Render to Canvas js Copy const { createCanvas, LottieAnimation } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) const canvas = createCanvas (animation. width , animation. height ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) // Render at original size animation. render (ctx) // Render with custom destination rect animation. render (ctx, { x : 0 , y : 0 , width : 800 , height : 600 }) Supported Features Embedded images - Base64-encoded images ( data:image/png;base64,... ) Embedded fonts - Vector glyph paths for text rendering without system fonts External assets - Load images from resourcePath directory dotLottie format - Extract .lottie ZIP files at runtime (see example) Example: Encode Lottie to Video See example/lottie-to-video.ts for encoding Lottie animations to MP4 using @napi-rs/webcodecs . js Copy import { createCanvas, LottieAnimation } from '@napi-rs/canvas' import { VideoEncoder , VideoFrame , Mp4Muxer , type EncodedVideoChunk , type EncodedVideoChunkMetadata , } from '@napi-rs/webcodecs' const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) const canvas = createCanvas (animation. width , animation. height ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) for ( let frame = 0 ; frame < animation. frames ; frame++) { animation. seekFrame (frame) ctx. fillStyle = '#ffffff' ctx. fillRect ( 0 , 0 , canvas. width , canvas. height ) animation. render (ctx) // Encode frame to video... } Example The tiger.json was serialized from gojs/samples/tiger shell Copy node example/anime-girl.js SVG PNG CC-BY-SA 3.0 by Niabot CC-BY-SA 3.0 by Niabot Building Build skia from source You can build this project from source, the system requirements are here: https://skia.org/docs/user/build sh Copy # Clone the code: $ git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Brooooooklyn/canvas.git $ cd canvas # Build Skia: $ node scripts/build-skia.js # Install NPM packages, build the Node.js addon: $ npm install -g yarn $ yarn install --mode=skip-build # `canvas` (node-canvas) is a native module that only the node-canvas compat tests use and is hard to install, you can skip building it by specifying `--mode=skip-build` $ sudo dnf install clang # https://fedora.pkgs.org/34/fedora-x86_64/clang-12.0.0-0.3.rc1.fc34.x86_64.rpm.html $ yarn build # All done! And there may be some bugs. For details on planned features and future direction please refer to the Roadmap . 中文文档 Install bash Copy yarn add @napi-rs/canvas npm install @napi-rs/canvas Support matrix System requirement arm64 cortex-a57 or newer CPU architecture on Linux . All Apple M chips on macOS . armv7 cortex-a7 or newer CPU architecture. glibc Since Skia relies on the glibc 2.18 API, you need to have at least glibc version >= 2.18 on your system. AWS Lambda usage To use this library on Lambda you will need to use a Lambda layer. You can simply attach a lambda layer by getting an ARN from Canvas-Lambda-Layer Make sure to exclude @napi-rs/canvas while bundling your Lambda. Usage js Copy const { promises } = require ( 'node:fs' ) const { join } = require ( 'node:path' ) const { createCanvas, loadImage } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) const canvas = createCanvas ( 300 , 320 ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) ctx. lineWidth = 10 ctx. strokeStyle = '#03a9f4' ctx. fillStyle = '#03a9f4' // Wall ctx. strokeRect ( 75 , 140 , 150 , 110 ) // Door ctx. fillRect ( 130 , 190 , 40 , 60 ) // Roof ctx. beginPath () ctx. moveTo ( 50 , 140 ) ctx. lineTo ( 150 , 60 ) ctx. lineTo ( 250 , 140 ) ctx. closePath () ctx. stroke () async function main ( ) { // load images from disk or from a URL const catImage = await loadImage ( 'path/to/cat.png' ) const dogImage = await loadImage ( 'https://example.com/path/to/dog.jpg' ) ctx. drawImage (catImage, 0 , 0 , catImage. width , catImage. height ) ctx. drawImage (dogImage, canvas. width / 2 , canvas. height / 2 , dogImage. width , dogImage. height ) // export canvas as image const pngData = await canvas. encode ( 'png' ) // JPEG, AVIF and WebP are also supported // encoding in libuv thread pool, non-blocking await promises. writeFile ( join (__dirname, 'simple.png' ), pngData) } main () Emoji text js Copy const { writeFileSync } = require ( 'fs' ) const { join } = require ( 'path' ) const { createCanvas, GlobalFonts } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) GlobalFonts . registerFromPath ( join (__dirname, '..' , 'fonts' , 'AppleColorEmoji@2x.ttf' ), 'Apple Emoji' ) GlobalFonts . registerFromPath ( join (__dirname, '..' , '__test__' , 'fonts' , 'COLRv1.ttf' ), 'COLRv1' ) console . info ( GlobalFonts . families ) const canvas = createCanvas ( 760 , 360 ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) ctx. font = '50px Apple Emoji' ctx. strokeText ( '😀😃😄😁😆😅😂🤣☺️😊😊😇' , 50 , 150 ) ctx. font = '100px COLRv1' ctx. fillText ( 'abc' , 50 , 300 ) const b = canvas. toBuffer ( 'image/png' ) writeFileSync ( join (__dirname, 'draw-emoji.png' ), b) Performance See benchmark for benchmark code. pages.b: pdf-parse Pure TypeScript, cross-platform module for extracting text, images, and tables from PDFs. Run 🤗 directly in your browser or in Node! Getting Started with v2 (Coming from v1) js Copy // v1 // const pdf = require('pdf-parse'); // pdf(buffer).then(result => console.log(result.text)); // v2 const { PDFParse } = require ( 'pdf-parse' ); // import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse'; async function run ( ) { const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : 'https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf' }); const result = await parser. getText (); console . log (result. text ); } run (); Features CJS, ESM, Node.js, and browser support. Can be integrated with React , Vue , Angular , or any other web framework. Command-line interface for quick PDF processing: CLI Documentation Security Policy Retrieve headers and validate PDF : [ getHeader ]( #getheader--node-utility-pdf-header-retrieval-and-validation ) Extract document info : [ getInfo ]( #getinfo--extract-metadata-and-document-information ) Extract page text : [ getText ]( #gettext--extract-text ) Render pages as PNG : [ getScreenshot ]( #getscreenshot--render-pages-as-png ) Extract embedded images : [ getImage ]( #getimage--extract-embedded-images ) Detect and extract tabular data : [ getTable ]( #gettable--extract-tabular-data ) Well-covered with unit tests Integration tests to validate end-to-end behavior across environments. See LoadParameters and ParseParameters for all available options. Examples: live demo , examples , tests and tests example folders. Supports: Next.js + Vercel , Netlify, AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers. Installation sh Copy npm install pdf-parse # or pnpm add pdf-parse # or yarn add pdf-parse # or bun add pdf-parse CLI Installation For command-line usage, install the package globally: sh Copy npm install -g pdf-parse Or use it directly with npx: sh Copy npx pdf-parse -- help For detailed CLI documentation and usage examples, see: CLI Documentation Usage getHeader — Node Utility: PDF Header Retrieval and Validation js Copy // Important: getHeader is available from the 'pdf-parse/node' submodule import { getHeader } from 'pdf-parse/node' ; // Retrieve HTTP headers and file size without downloading the full file. // Pass `true` to check PDF magic bytes via range request. // Optionally validates PDFs by fetching the first 4 bytes (magic bytes). // Useful for checking file existence, size, and type before full parsing. // Node only, will not work in browser environments. const result = await getHeader ( 'https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf' , true ); console . log ( `Status: ${result.status} ` ); console . log ( `Content-Length: ${result.size} ` ); console . log ( `Is PDF: ${result.isPdf} ` ); console . log ( `Headers:` , result. headers ); getInfo — Extract Metadata and Document Information js Copy import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse' ; const link = 'https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/pdf/climate.pdf' ; // const buffer = await readFile('reports/pdf/climate.pdf'); // const parser = new PDFParse({ data: buffer }); const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : link }); const result = await parser. getInfo ({ parsePageInfo : true }); await parser. destroy (); console . log ( `Total pages: ${result.total} ` ); console . log ( `Title: ${result.info?.Title} ` ); console . log ( `Author: ${result.info?.Author} ` ); console . log ( `Creator: ${result.info?.Creator} ` ); console . log ( `Producer: ${result.info?.Producer} ` ); // Access parsed date information const dates = result. getDateNode (); console . log ( `Creation Date: ${dates.CreationDate} ` ); console . log ( `Modification Date: ${dates.ModDate} ` ); // Links, pageLabel, width, height (when `parsePageInfo` is true) console . log ( 'Per-page information:' ); console . log ( JSON . stringify (result. pages , null , 2 )); getText — Extract Text js Copy import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse' ; const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : 'https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf' }); const result = await parser. getText (); // to extract text from page 3 only: // const result = await parser.getText({ partial: [3] }); await parser. destroy (); console . log (result. text ); For a complete list of configuration options, see: LoadParameters ParseParameters Usage Examples: Parse password protected PDF: password.test.ts Parse only specific pages: specific-pages.test.ts Parse embedded hyperlinks: hyperlink.test.ts Set verbosity level: password.test.ts Load PDF from URL: url.test.ts Load PDF from base64 data: base64.test.ts Loading large files (> 5 MB): large-file.test.ts getScreenshot — Render Pages as PNG js Copy import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse' ; const link = 'https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf' ; // const buffer = await readFile('reports/pdf/bitcoin.pdf'); // const parser = new PDFParse({ data: buffer }); const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : link }); // scale:1 for original page size. // scale:1.5 50% bigger. const result = await parser. getScreenshot ({ scale : 1.5 }); await parser. destroy (); await writeFile ( 'bitcoin.png' , result. pages [ 0 ]. data ); Usage Examples: Limit output resolution or specific pages using ParseParameters getScreenshot({scale:1.5}) — Increase rendering scale (higher DPI / larger image) getScreenshot({desiredWidth:1024}) — Request a target width in pixels; height scales to keep aspect ratio imageDataUrl (default: true ) — include base64 data URL string in the result. imageBuffer (default: true ) — include a binary buffer for each image. Select specific pages with partial (e.g. getScreenshot({ partial: [1,3] }) ) partial overrides first / last . Use first to render the first N pages (e.g. getScreenshot({ first: 3 }) ). Use last to render the last N pages (e.g. getScreenshot({ last: 2 }) ). When both first and last are provided they form an inclusive range ( first..last ). getImage — Extract Embedded Images js Copy import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse' ; const link = new URL ( 'https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/pdf/image-test.pdf' ); // const buffer = await readFile('reports/pdf/image-test.pdf'); // const parser = new PDFParse({ data: buffer }); const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : link }); const result = await parser. getImage (); await parser. destroy (); await writeFile ( 'adobe.png' , result. pages [ 0 ]. images [ 0 ]. data ); Usage Examples: Exclude images with width or height <= 50 px: getImage({ imageThreshold: 50 }) Default imageThreshold is 80 (pixels) Useful for excluding tiny decorative or tracking images. To disable size-based filtering and include all images, set imageThreshold: 0 . imageDataUrl (default: true ) — include base64 data URL string in the result. imageBuffer (default: true ) — include a binary buffer for each image. Extract images from specific pages: getImage({ partial: [2,4] }) getTable — Extract Tabular Data js Copy import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' ; import { PDFParse } from 'pdf-parse' ; const link = new URL ( 'https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/pdf/simple-table.pdf' ); // const buffer = await readFile('reports/pdf/simple-table.pdf'); // const parser = new PDFParse({ data: buffer }); const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : link }); const result = await parser. getTable (); await parser. destroy (); // Pretty-print each row of the first table for ( const row of result. pages [ 0 ]. tables [ 0 ]) { console . log ( JSON . stringify (row)); } Exception Handling & Type Usage ts Copy import type { LoadParameters , ParseParameters , TextResult } from 'pdf-parse' ; import { PasswordException , PDFParse , VerbosityLevel } from 'pdf-parse' ; const loadParams : LoadParameters = { url : 'https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/pdf/password-123456.pdf' , verbosity : VerbosityLevel . WARNINGS , password : 'abcdef' , }; const parseParams : ParseParameters = { first : 1 , }; // Initialize the parser class without executing any code yet const parser = new PDFParse (loadParams); function handleResult ( result : TextResult ) { console . log (result. text ); } try { const result = await parser. getText (parseParams); handleResult (result); } catch (error) { // InvalidPDFException // PasswordException // FormatError // ResponseException // AbortException // UnknownErrorException if (error instanceof PasswordException ) { console . error ( 'Password must be 123456\n' , error); } else { throw error; } } finally { // Always call destroy() to free memory await parser. destroy (); } Web / Browser Can be integrated into React , Vue , Angular , or any other web framework. Live Demo: https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/ Demo Source: reports/demo ES Module : pdf-parse.es.js UMD/Global : pdf-parse.umd.js For browser build, set the web worker explicitly. CDN Usage html Copy <!-- ES Module --> < script type = "module" > import { PDFParse } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf-parse.es.js' ; //// Available Worker Files // pdf.worker.mjs // pdf.worker.min.mjs // If you use a custom build or host pdf.worker.mjs yourself, configure worker accordingly. PDFParse . setWorker ( 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf.worker.mjs' ); const parser = new PDFParse ({ url : 'https://mehmet-kozan.github.io/pdf-parse/pdf/bitcoin.pdf' }); const result = await parser. getText (); console . log (result. text ) </ script > **CDN Options: https://www.jsdelivr.com/package/npm/pdf-parse** https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf-parse.es.js https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@2.4.5/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf-parse.es.js https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf-parse.umd.js https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@2.4.5/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf-parse.umd.js Worker Options: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf.worker.mjs https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pdf-parse@latest/dist/pdf-parse/web/pdf.worker.min.mjs Similar Packages pdf2json — Buggy, memory leaks, uncatchable errors in some PDF files. pdfdataextract — pdf-parse -based unpdf — pdf-parse -based pdf-extract — Non-cross-platform, depends on xpdf j-pdfjson — Fork of pdf2json pdfreader — Uses pdf2json pdf-extract — Non-cross-platform, depends on xpdf Benchmark Note: The benchmark currently runs only against pdf2json . I don't know the current state of pdf2json — the original reason for creating pdf-parse was to work around stability issues with pdf2json . I deliberately did not include pdf-parse or other pdf.js -based packages in the benchmark because dependencies conflict. If you have recommendations for additional packages to include, please open an issue, see benchmark results . Supported Node.js Versions(20.x, 22.x, 23.x, 24.x) Supported: Node.js 20 (>= 20.16.0), Node.js 22 (>= 22.3.0), Node.js 23 (>= 23.0.0), and Node.js 24 (>= 24.0.0). Not supported: Node.js 21.x, and Node.js 19.x and earlier. Integration tests run on Node.js 20–24, see test_integration.yml . And there may be some bugs. For details on planned features and future direction please refer to the Roadmap . 中文文档 Install bash Copy yarn add @napi-rs/canvas npm install @napi-rs/canvas Support matrix System requirement arm64 cortex-a57 or newer CPU architecture on Linux . All Apple M chips on macOS . armv7 cortex-a7 or newer CPU architecture. glibc Since Skia relies on the glibc 2.18 API, you need to have at least glibc version >= 2.18 on your system. AWS Lambda usage To use this library on Lambda you will need to use a Lambda layer. You can simply attach a lambda layer by getting an ARN from Canvas-Lambda-Layer Make sure to exclude @napi-rs/canvas while bundling your Lambda. Usage js Copy const { promises } = require ( 'node:fs' ) const { join } = require ( 'node:path' ) const { createCanvas, loadImage } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) const canvas = createCanvas ( 300 , 320 ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) ctx. lineWidth = 10 ctx. strokeStyle = '#03a9f4' ctx. fillStyle = '#03a9f4' // Wall ctx. strokeRect ( 75 , 140 , 150 , 110 ) // Door ctx. fillRect ( 130 , 190 , 40 , 60 ) // Roof ctx. beginPath () ctx. moveTo ( 50 , 140 ) ctx. lineTo ( 150 , 60 ) ctx. lineTo ( 250 , 140 ) ctx. closePath () ctx. stroke () async function main ( ) { // load images from disk or from a URL const catImage = await loadImage ( 'path/to/cat.png' ) const dogImage = await loadImage ( 'https://example.com/path/to/dog.jpg' ) ctx. drawImage (catImage, 0 , 0 , catImage. width , catImage. height ) ctx. drawImage (dogImage, canvas. width / 2 , canvas. height / 2 , dogImage. width , dogImage. height ) // export canvas as image const pngData = await canvas. encode ( 'png' ) // JPEG, AVIF and WebP are also supported // encoding in libuv thread pool, non-blocking await promises. writeFile ( join (__dirname, 'simple.png' ), pngData) } main () Emoji text js Copy const { writeFileSync } = require ( 'fs' ) const { join } = require ( 'path' ) const { createCanvas, GlobalFonts } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) GlobalFonts . registerFromPath ( join (__dirname, '..' , 'fonts' , 'AppleColorEmoji@2x.ttf' ), 'Apple Emoji' ) GlobalFonts . registerFromPath ( join (__dirname, '..' , '__test__' , 'fonts' , 'COLRv1.ttf' ), 'COLRv1' ) console . info ( GlobalFonts . families ) const canvas = createCanvas ( 760 , 360 ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) ctx. font = '50px Apple Emoji' ctx. strokeText ( '😀😃😄😁😆😅😂🤣☺️😊😊😇' , 50 , 150 ) ctx. font = '100px COLRv1' ctx. fillText ( 'abc' , 50 , 300 ) const b = canvas. toBuffer ( 'image/png' ) writeFileSync ( join (__dirname, 'draw-emoji.png' ), b) Performance See benchmark for benchmark code. Load Animation js Copy const { LottieAnimation } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) // Load from file const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) // Load from JSON string with resource path for external assets const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromData (jsonString, { resourcePath : '/path/to/assets' , }) Animation Properties js Copy animation. duration // Total duration in seconds animation. fps // Frames per second animation. frames // Total frame count animation. width // Animation width animation. height // Animation height animation. version // Lottie format version Playback Control js Copy animation. seekFrame ( 30 ) // Seek to frame 30 animation. seek ( 1.5 ) // Seek to 1.5 seconds Render to Canvas js Copy const { createCanvas, LottieAnimation } = require ( '@napi-rs/canvas' ) const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) const canvas = createCanvas (animation. width , animation. height ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) // Render at original size animation. render (ctx) // Render with custom destination rect animation. render (ctx, { x : 0 , y : 0 , width : 800 , height : 600 }) Supported Features Embedded images - Base64-encoded images ( data:image/png;base64,... ) Embedded fonts - Vector glyph paths for text rendering without system fonts External assets - Load images from resourcePath directory dotLottie format - Extract .lottie ZIP files at runtime (see example) Example: Encode Lottie to Video See example/lottie-to-video.ts for encoding Lottie animations to MP4 using @napi-rs/webcodecs . js Copy import { createCanvas, LottieAnimation } from '@napi-rs/canvas' import { VideoEncoder , VideoFrame , Mp4Muxer , type EncodedVideoChunk , type EncodedVideoChunkMetadata , } from '@napi-rs/webcodecs' const animation = LottieAnimation . loadFromFile ( 'animation.json' ) const canvas = createCanvas (animation. width , animation. height ) const ctx = canvas. getContext ( '2d' ) for ( let frame = 0 ; Debug artifacts (smoke tests, probe logs, AE boot logs) are intentionally kept. Scene timing: intro 0-5, hero 5-12, essentials 12-18, shop 18-27, cart 27-34, payments 34-45, order+pipeline 45-53, account 53-57, end card 57-60. No render, no quit — the user adds sound themselves. Hardened vs v1: no app.newProject() (the call that crashed AE headless), null-fill-safe shape helper, log + alert with paths on any error. v1 ( build_promo.jsx ) stays untouched as an artifact. To run it again any time: AE File > Scripts > Run Script File… → promo-build\build_promo_v2.jsx (run it once per fresh AE session; running twice stacks duplicate comps in the same project — harmless but messy). Adding sound (the user's workflow): File > Import > File… → pick music (mp3/wav) drag it into the Estrera Promo 60s timeline below the video layers , at 0:00 trim/fade to taste (60s; the end card starts at 57s — fade out under it) File > Export > Add to Adobe Media Encoder Queue → H.264, 1920×1080, 30fps If text shows in a wrong font instead of DM Serif Display / Plus Jakarta Sans (postScriptName resolution is AE-version picky): select the text layers, pick DM Serif Display / Plus Jakarta Sans in the character panel — everything is already placed/timed, only the face may need a swap. The build log records which postScriptName each family resolved to. After Effects headless + one-click fallback (original, for the record) AE 2026 headless ( -noui -r ) crashes at app.newProject() on this machine (exit 1, GPU3 warning in stderr) and -r scripts are silently refused — that's why the canvas pipeline carries the video deliverable. build_promo.jsx (v1) remains as the AE-native design source it was written from. The bootstrap opencode_promo_build.jsx in AE's Scripts\Startup folder is flag-gated: it does nothing unless promo-build\run_now.flag exists. render/ae_boot_seen.txt proves the bootstrap ran on any AE launch. House rules honored No file is deleted by this pipeline; superseded artifacts are kept (zip, debug logs, both test scripts). Attention: python notify.py "OpenCode" "message" — launched only via detached Start-Process so it doesn't block the shell. Master comp Estrera Promo v4 60s (1920x1080 30fps 60s) + 9 scene comps; 5 page precomps + 3 modal precomps (1400x854/3020x1250, canvas-local coords) carry all interaction keyframes at v4's exact times; real shape/text layers, browser chrome (bar mask r18, tab-strip masks, viewport matte), cursor rigs with hand/arrow swap + ripples. Re-run: write run_now.flag (content = build_promo_v4_native.jsx ) in the promo-build folder, then restart AE - the Startup bootstrap evals it. Watch with render/watch_v4_native.ps1 (log render/build_v4_native_log.txt ; success = DONE. + AEP exists). Run once per fresh AE session (duplicate comps otherwise). AE scripting traps encoded in the script (do not regress): Shape attrs validate on assignment: build local arrays, assign once. Mask add: Masks.addProperty("ADBE Mask Atom") , path via ADBE Mask Shape . layer.parent = X is world-preserving (offsets frozen at set time) - parent BEFORE keying the parent's motion (pipeline/cursor rigs rely on this). addProperty on an indexed group invalidates sibling property refs - re-fetch before keying (intro rule). Dashes: add ADBE Vector Stroke Dash/Gap 1 items before setting values. 2D properties (Scale/Position) need array values, never scalars. Music + export: same as the v4 pipeline (add audio in Estrera Promo v4 60s at 0:00, fade ~0:57, Add to Adobe Media Encoder Queue, H.264 1920x1080 30fps). pages.b: Instructions Form groups of 3 - 4 students. Each group will assume the roles involved in a systems integration project: Note: Each member of the group will be assigned any of this responsibilities. Project Manager IT Systems Lead Business Unit Manager End-user Representative Each group selects or is assigned a fictional project, such as: University Student System Hospital Management System Laboratory Information System Small retail POS + Inventory System + E-commerce System As a group, simulate a planning session. Discuss and document: Each role’s responsibilities and concerns Potential organizational issues, such as: Resistance to new technology Poor communication between departments Conflicting priorities Lack of user training Budget/timeline constraints Individual Reflection Paper Propose solutions or best practices to address these challenges in paragraph format. Discuss in paragraph what were the main managerial/organizational issues discussed during the group discussion. How did your group resolve role conflicts or challenges? What are the real-world implications of these issues in actual IT projects? What best practices would you recommend for IT managers leading integration projects? My Role Project Manager Context traffic allocated money student staff Resolution of Role Conflicts and Challenges Proposed Solutions and Best Practices for Organizational Challenges Real-World Implications of Organizational Issues in Actual IT Projects Recommended Best Practices for IT Managers Leading Integration Projects Project The Project will be a University Student System University Student System - Integration Project Planning 1. Project Overview Project Name: University Student System Integration Project My Role: Project Manager 2. Roles, Responsibilities, and Concerns Project Manager (My Role) Responsibilities: Oversee the entire integration project from initiation to closure. Manage the allocated money, ensure timelines align with the academic calendar, and act as the bridge between technical teams, administration, and end-users. Concerns: Staying within strict budget constraints, scope creep, ensuring all departments are aligned, and preventing timeline delays that could disrupt the upcoming semester. IT Systems Lead Responsibilities: Design the technical architecture, handle data migration from legacy systems, ensure system security, and guarantee the infrastructure can handle high traffic (e.g., thousands of students accessing the system simultaneously during enrollment). Concerns: Technical debt from old legacy systems, server crashes during peak traffic, data breaches, and integrating disjointed databases (e.g., financial and academic records). Business Unit Manager (e.g., University Registrar/Finance Admin) Responsibilities: Ensure the new system correctly enforces university policies, handles financial transactions accurately, and provides necessary reporting tools for the staff. Concerns: Disruption to daily administrative operations during the transition, data corruption during migration, and the possibility that the allocated money won't cover essential operational features. End-user Representative (Student & Faculty Liaison) Responsibilities: Advocate for the needs of students and teaching staff. Test the system for usability, accessibility, and intuitive design. Concerns: A steep learning curve, confusing interfaces, system downtime during critical periods (like submitting grades or paying tuition), and lack of proper onboarding. 3. Potential Organizational Issues Resistance to new technology: Many university staff members and veteran professors may be accustomed to the legacy system or paper-based processes. They may view the new system as an unnecessary complication rather than an upgrade. we can use a a paper based protocol. in the paper based protocol, what the veteran staff will do is they get the necessary printed papers, fill those up and scan it with an interpreter software so that the physical document is read and turned into digital automatically. they can also edit the document if there are some things the interpreter could not read but if they still wouldn't get it, there will be another staff that will help them with the protocol if they need help with it. Poor communication between departments: The IT department might use technical jargon that the Business Unit Managers (Registrar/Finance) do not understand. Conversely, IT might not fully grasp the intricate academic rules and prerequisites needed for the system. We can have a policy dealing with that. First for the poor communication with the Professionals. in the policy we will state that when talking to an employee with the same profession they can talk technically but when dealing with employees with different a profession, they have to talk in english rather than technically to avoid jargon. Conversely, for IT not getting the full grasp of academic rules and prerequisites. we will ask the university registrar the academic rules, the prerequisites, the student handbook and other things the system may need. Conflicting priorities: The IT Lead may want to delay the launch to ensure perfect system stability and handle high traffic seamlessly, whereas the Project Manager and Business Unit Manager are pressured to launch the system immediately before the next enrollment period begins. Since the university has an academic calendar, there are no excuses to delay the launch of the system before enrollment however, what we can do is to launch the system with a limit to its traffic, let the student be advised to refresh the page if it doesn't load and let the IT lead start a branch of the System so that they can address the high traffic issue. after fixing the high traffic issue, we can update the system quetly when there is little traffic like midnight Lack of user training: With thousands of students and hundreds of staff members, providing adequate training is a massive logistical challenge. Without it, users will struggle, leading to a flood of support tickets and frustration. Different groups need different levels of training staff who use the system daily need hands-on sessions, while students and faculty just need simple guides for the features they'll actually use. Skipping this step means people get confused, support teams get overwhelmed, and users may avoid the new system together, even if it works fine technically. That's why training should be planned and budgeted early, not added in at the last minute. Budget/timeline constraints: The project is bound by a fixed allocated money pool and a rigid academic calendar. Any delays or requirements for additional funds will require difficult trade-offs, such as cutting planned features (like a mobile app version) to launch on time. To handle these constraints without failing the project, we will adopt a phased rollout strategy based on a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) approach. We will allocate the budget to prioritize core functionalities needed for the immediate academic calendar—such as enrollment processing, student records, and basic finance—and push non-essential features, like the mobile app version, to a Phase 2 release. Reflection 1. Main Managerial and Organizational Issues Discussed During our group discussion, we found some critical managerial and organizational issues in regards to integrating a University Student System. first obstacle was the resistance to new technology among veteran staff members, they rely on legacy paper-based processes which doesn't really fit in the innovation of a new system. we also analyzed the poor comunnication between departments, mostly on the technical jargons that will arise when employees of different professions talk to each other and conversely, how IT lacks familiarity of the academic handbook rules and enrollment prerequisites. Moreover, we also encountered conflicting priorities between the IT Lead-who prioritized stability and high traffic controll but then the business administration faced pressure to launch the system before the academic deadline. lastly, we addressed the massive challenge of training thousands of students and staff members within the our allocated money and rigid calendar constraints 2. Proposed Solutions and Best Practices To solve these challenges, our group made practical, structured solutions for each issue. To minimize technology resistance, we designed a traditional paper-based protocol where where veteran staff complete printed forms that are audomatically digitalized using an OCR/interpreter software, supported by staff who will assist them whenever reading errors happen. To break down department communication barriers, we made a strict communication policy: Professionals must clear, non-technical english when coordinating across departments , and IT must directly reference the registrar's handbook for rule validation. now for user training. we made a tiered approach providing intensive hand on sessions for staff who will interact with the system daily while giving the students and faculty a quick-start guide to the system they will interact with. Finally, to manage financial and timeline constraints, we used a Minimum Viable Product or MVP strategy, focusing on core enrollment and record features while moving non-essential features like a mobile app to a future update or future phase. 3. Resolution of Role Conflicts and Challenges As a Project Manager, resolving problems between the IT Systems Lead and the Business Unit Manager regarding lunch readiness needed a collaborative approach. when we had our discussion session, we acknowledged that because the university operates on a fixed academic calendar, a delay or a launch beyond the enrollment was not an option. We found alternatives such as user queueing system but we realized it would cause unnecessary friction to the traffic. Drawing directly from our recent lessons on the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), all of us agreed to launch the working core system on the schedule time while handling initial high traffic by setting soft connection caps or limits and advising the students to refresh the webpage if there's some issues. at the same time the IT team developed a parallel branch to resolve server load issues and pushing small incremental updates during low-traffic hours (like midnight) so that students and staff will not notice the transition of the update and there will be no interruptions. 4. Real-World Implications of Organizational Issues The Organizational and techical issues discussed have real world consequences if left unmanaged. some major platforms like facebook and discord show that even a massive infrastructure can crash when hit with unexpected traffic spikes. in an academic setting, a total enrollmet crash will stall the registration and disrupts tuition collection and will also trigger a lot of public frustration. Miscommunications and overlooked technical security can also lead to catasrophic data breaches, just like the registrar API leaks seen in our university ( https://sms.norsu.top ). Furthermore, failing to consider for user training or budgetary limits often result to widepsread user rejection, abandoned software investments and severe administrative backlogs that will threaten the university's operational continuity. 5. Recommended Best Practices for IT Managers For IT managers leading complex systems integration project, theres some best practices things i recommend Enforce Plain-Language Communication: Make sure to have a clear cross-departmental communication to negate technical jargon and ensure technical requirements meet perfectly with operational and academic policies Adopt and Agile and Phased Deployment Strategy: Focus on initial releases on an MVP to satisfy strict calendar deadlines, using continuous, incremantal updates during low traffic hours to improve system performance without causing downtime Implement Strict Change Control and Prioritization: protect allocated money and timeline by prioritizing core functions needed by primary stakeholders before considering extra enhancements. Prioritize Early Security and Traffic Testing: start rigorous load testing and API security audits early on in the development life cycle to prevent high traffic crashes and data culnerabilities before a public launch

pages.b: Classwork 1: The 7 Phases of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) Instructions Read the Discussion: Read the discussion about the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) before answering the activity. Reference: IBM Think – What is the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)? Complete All Parts: Complete Parts I to III of this activity. Independent Work: Answer all questions independently using your own understanding. Clarity: Write your answers clearly and completely. Format Requirement: Convert your file into a PDF format before submission. Deadline: Submit your completed activity on or before July 24, 2026 (Friday) . Part I. Identification Directions Write the correct SDLC phase described in each statement. Establishes project goals, scope, feasibility, and risks. Answer: Planning Phase Gathers functional and non-functional requirements from stakeholders. Answer: Analysis Phase Creates system architecture, interface designs, and workflows. Answer: Design Phase Develops the actual software using programming languages. Answer: Coding Phase / development phase Ensures the software meets quality standards through testing. Answer: Testing Releases the completed software to users. Answer: Deployment phase Provides updates, bug fixes, and continuous improvements. Answer: Maintenance Phase Part II. Scenario-Based Scenario Context Your university wants to develop an Online Student Clearance System that allows students to complete their clearance digitally. Task Complete the table below by identifying what activities should be performed during each SDLC phase for this project. SDLC Phase Example Activity Planning Defining project scope, budget and deadlines Requirement Analysis Gathering clearance rules from university departments Design Creating screen mockups and database layouts Development Coding the web portal and approval database Testing Checking for bugs and login issues Deployment Launching the portal live on university servers Maintenance Fixing errors and updating features overtime Part III. Reflection Directions Answer the following questions in 3–5 sentences each. 1. Why is Requirement Analysis considered one of the most important phases of the SDLC? Answer Requirement analysis shows the exact goals, features and constraints of the software before any design or coding starts. Knowing stakeholder needs early will prevent expensive rework, project delays, and misunderstandings in the development cycle. It also gives the needed blueprint that guides the design, development and testing tasks 2. What problems might occur if the Testing phase is skipped before deployment? Answer The software might have bugs when it is deployed. Many customers or users will have many complaints on said bugs. Customers may stop using your software because it has proven that it's unreliable to them because of the bugs that were overlooked.

Scenario A university wants an Online Student Advising System so students can request academic advising, view advisor availability, schedule appointments, and receive advising notes. Actors: Student, Academic Advisor, and Administrator. Key high-level functions: submit advising request, check advisor schedules, book/reschedule/cancel an appointment, and view/download advising notes. Instruction Create a Use Case Diagram in (e.g. Lucidchart or Draw.io) showing actors and main use cases (e.g., Submit Request, View Advisor Availability, Book Appointment, Reschedule/Cancel Appointment, Upload/View Advising Notes, Admin: Manage Advisors/Schedules). Create a Activity Diagram in (e.g. Lucidchart or Draw.io) describing the workflow for “Student books an advising appointment” from start to finish include decision points (e.g., advisor available?), parallel actions (notify advisor + update calendar), and end states. Submit diagrams as PNG or PDF and include a 200–300 word explanation for each diagram describing your assumptions. Use Case Diagram The Use Case Diagram shows the scope and user interactions inside the Online Student Advising system across 3 primary factors being the "Student", the "Academic Advisor, and the "Administrator". The student is the primary end user who starts core self-service functions, including submitting advising requests, viewing advisor free time, making appointments, rescheduling or cancelling existing appointments and also viewing or downloading advising notes. The Academic Advisor will interact with the system to review schedules, access student records and also upload official advising notes to following sessions. Lastly, the Administrator maintains system infrastructure by managing advisor profiles, roster assignments and also operational availability schedules. Activity Diagram Some Key design assumptions control this structure. The first being, user authentication is considered as a prerequisite for all interaction. actors must securely log in before accessing all or any features, keeping security concerns small rather than cluttering the functional diagram. Second, data access must be strictly controlled by role-based permissions to ensure privacy. Students need to only possess read-only permissions for their personal advising notes, and Advisers are granted edit access to upload their notes only for their assigned advice. Third, system updates such as appointment bookings or cancellations will automatically trigger notification services to keep both sites be it students and advisors be informed without needing secondary actor interaction. and finally, administrative control over advisor schedules establishes the baseline operational hours in which individual advisors can setup their availability-

Form a group of 3-5 members Estrera Academia Orcullo Tejeros Leon system name Lavhanan Laundry Hub. The name of our project is the "Lavhanan Laundry Hub (Laundry hub management system)." We chose this name simply because it is the original name given by the business owner. Our main goal is to support the owner and help their business grow by bringing it online. We are not trying to change their shop, but rather extend it with new digital tools. By adding this online computer system, we want to make their daily work easier, keep their records more organized, and give their customers a better and faster way to track their laundry. Problem to be solved The Lavhanan laundry business has a few main problems that the new computer system needs to solve. First, the staff writes all the customer orders by hand in a logbook and uses small paper receipts, which makes it hard to keep detailed records. Second, because they do not usually count every piece of clothing, some customers try to claim that their items are missing or lost. Third, when people do not pay or forget to pick up their laundry, the workers have to manually search for the customer's phone number on paper and call them one by one. Fourth, adding up the daily sales is done by hand, which can be slow and difficult to manage. Finally, customers do not have a way to know exactly when their clothes are ready for pickup. The new system will fix these problems by saving all the information online, tracking exact item counts, calculating the daily money automatically, and sending automatic text messages directly to the customers. Target users The target users for the Lavhanan Laundry Hub are divided into two main groups: Employees and Customers. Here is a simple breakdown of how each role will use the system: Lavhanan Employees (Admin and Staff) Owner / Admin: Has full control over the computer system. They can see all the daily money earned, read the monthly sales reports, and manage the accounts for all other workers. Manager: Helps the owner watch over the daily business. They can look at all the laundry orders, make sure the work is not slow, and fix any big problems with the customers. Cashier: Welcomes the customer and takes the dirty laundry. They type the customer's name into the system, weigh the clothes, give the receipt, and mark the order as "paid" or "unpaid." Labandera (Laundry Worker): Does the physical washing. They use the system to simply update the steps of the laundry (clicking buttons to show if the clothes are washing, drying, folding, or ready). Delivery Driver: Uses the system to see the customer's home address and updates the app when the clean clothes are dropped off. (Even if the shop only does pickups right now, this prepares the system for the future). Lavhanan Customers People who bring their clothes to the shop. They use the simple online web app on their phones to check if their laundry is ready, see how much they need to pay, and ask the shop for help if they need it. Major System Functions Functional Features (What the system actually does) Record Orders Online: The cashier can type the customer's name, the weight of the clothes, and the price into the computer instead of writing in a paper book. Track Laundry Steps: The workers (Labandera) can click simple buttons to show what is happening to the clothes, like moving them from "Washing" to "Drying" to "Ready." Count Specific Clothes: The system can record the exact number and type of clothes for certain customers. This stops people from saying the shop lost their items. Track Payments: The system will save if an order is "Paid" or "Unpaid," which makes it very easy to handle "wash now, pay later" customers. Send Automatic Text Messages: The system will automatically send an SMS to the customer when their clothes are ready, if there is a power outage, or if they forgot to pick up their clothes. Calculate Daily Sales (Reports): The system will automatically add up all the money the shop made in a day or a month, so the owner does not have to do the math by hand. Customer Online Checker: Customers can use a simple web page on their phones to check if their laundry is finished. Non-Functional Features (How the system behaves and feels) Easy to Use (User-Friendly): The app will be very simple. Workers only need to learn a few clicks, and customers will have a very easy screen to look at. Safe and Secure: The information is protected. Customers can only see their own laundry, and only the Owner or Admin can look at the daily money and reports. Mobile-Friendly: The customer app and the delivery driver features will work smoothly and look good on small smartphone screens. Fast and Reliable: When a worker clicks a button to say the laundry is done, the system updates quickly so the customer gets the text message right away. Information/Data needed To make the new computer system work, it needs to collect and save specific everyday information. First, we need basic customer details, like their names and phone numbers, so the system can send them text messages. Second, we need laundry details for every single order. This includes the weight of the clothes, the exact number of clothing items (to stop customers from saying things are missing), and any special washing instructions. Third, we need money details, which means recording the total price and saving if the customer has already "paid" or if the order is still "unpaid." Finally, the system needs tracking details to remember exactly what step the clothes are in like washing, drying, or ready for pickup—and worker details to know which employee is doing the job. Expected System Outputs (What we will build) The final project will be delivered in two ways: a Web App (Website) and an Android App . Both the Lavhanan employees and the customers will be able to log in and use both of these platforms to check their laundry or do their work. System Constraints (Limitations) We cannot build an iOS (Apple/iPhone) version of the mobile app. This is because the specific programming tools (framework) we are using to build the project only support Android. However, this is not a big problem because iPhone users—whether they are employees or customers—can simply open the Web App on their phone's internet browser to use the system perfectly fine. Security Requirements To keep the business and customer information safe, the system will have strict security rules. First, everyone using the app must log in with a secure password so strangers cannot get inside. Second, the system will use strict access limits based on exactly who is logging in. Customers can only see their own laundry tickets and cannot look at other people's phone numbers. For the employees, normal workers can only see and update the laundry orders they are working on. The Manager is given a middle level of access; they can see all of the laundry orders and customer details to help solve shop problems, but they cannot change the most private system settings. Finally, only the Owner or Admin is allowed to see the big financial sales reports and the total money earned. The system will also protect the records by stopping anyone from accidentally deleting an order, especially if the customer still has an "unpaid" bill. Other Requirements/Constraints There are a few other important rules and limits for this project. First, the business owner actually owns the computer server and keeps it right at the laundry shop. Because the server is nearby, the workers can still use the system on the shop's local Wi-Fi even if the outside internet is slow or goes down. However, the shop will still need some internet connection to send the automatic text messages and to let customers check their laundry from their own homes. Second, the new computer system must be able to connect to a thermal receipt printer, so the shop can keep printing small paper tags for the laundry baskets. Third, the workers and the manager must use Android phones, Android tablets, or a normal computer, since there is no Apple iPhone version. Finally, the system must include a very simple video tutorial so everyone can easily learn how to use the new app. Copy expected system output would be webapp or website and android app. the constraint is we can't develop ios version because the framework we will use is for android both can be used by employees and customers
